course.title: Statistical and Causal Inference
course.description: From the wobble of a sample mean to a defensible claim about cause. Intervals, tests, power, regression, experiments and causal diagrams.
course.audience: A capable adult who has met means, spread and sampling in Discere's probability course and wants to know how far a result can be trusted and when it shows cause.

paragraphs: Every number computed from a sample, whether a mean, a proportion or the slope of a line, would have come out a little differently had another sample been drawn. Statistical inference is the study of how much that difference matters. It describes the spread a result would show across every sample that could have been taken, and that spread turns a bare estimate such as a mean of 52 into a statement that can be judged, such as an interval of about 49 to 55 from a method that misses the true value about one time in twenty.

A well-measured result can still answer the wrong question. Ice cream sales and drownings rise and fall together through the year, and a line fitted through them rises too, yet no one supposes that ice cream drowns anyone, because hot weather raises both. Causal inference is the study of what must be true of the way data came about before a difference between groups can be read as the effect of something, and the answer depends on how the groups were formed, since groups that chose their own treatment can differ in ways the data never recorded.

Read together, the two halves give a way to examine any claim that something works or causes something. One question asks how much of the result could be chance, and the other asks how much could be something else that nobody measured. The first can be answered with arithmetic on the numbers a study reports, and the second with careful reasoning about how those numbers came to be collected.
outcomes: You'll be able to build and read a confidence interval for a mean, a proportion and a difference.
You'll be able to run a test and say what its p-value does and does not mean.
You'll be able to judge whether a study had enough data and whether many tests inflated its results.
You'll be able to fit a line and refuse to read it as a cause.
You'll be able to explain why randomising works, spot a confounder and use a causal diagram to choose what to adjust for.

modules.title: Estimating with honest uncertainty
modules.description: From the way sample means vary to intervals that say how far a result can be trusted.

modules.title: Testing claims
modules.description: What a p-value is, the two ways a test can fail, how many observations a test needs, and the trap of running many tests.

concepts.title: Sampling distribution
concepts.summary: The distribution of a statistic, such as a sample mean, over all the samples of one size that could be drawn.

concepts.title: Standard error
concepts.summary: The standard deviation of a sample mean, equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of n.

concepts.title: z-score
concepts.summary: The number of standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean: z = (x - mean) / sd.

concepts.title: Normal model
concepts.summary: A symmetric bell-shaped distribution fully described by its mean and standard deviation, with fixed areas at fixed z-scores.

concepts.title: Margin of error
concepts.summary: The critical value times the standard error; the half-width of the interval.

concepts.title: t critical value
concepts.summary: The multiplier used when the population sd is unknown and estimated by s; it is larger than the z value for small samples.

concepts.title: Coverage
concepts.summary: The long-run share of intervals, made by the same method on repeated samples, that contain the true value.

concepts.title: Proportion interval
concepts.summary: p-hat plus or minus a critical value times sqrt(p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n).

concepts.title: p-value
concepts.summary: The probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.

concepts.title: Null hypothesis
concepts.summary: A specific default claim, such as a mean equal to 100, against which the data are measured.

concepts.title: Type I error
concepts.summary: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is true; its rate is the significance level alpha.

concepts.title: Power
concepts.summary: The probability of rejecting the null when a specific alternative is true; one minus the missed-effect rate.

concepts.title: Effect size
concepts.summary: The difference worth detecting, often compared with the standard deviation.

concepts.title: Sample size for power
concepts.summary: n = ((z_alpha/2 + z_beta) x sigma / delta)^2 for a two-sided test of a mean.

concepts.title: Interval for a difference
concepts.summary: (mean1 - mean2) +/- critical x sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2) for independent groups.

concepts.title: Paired design
concepts.summary: Two measurements on the same unit; analyse the differences as one sample.

concepts.title: Family-wise error
concepts.summary: The probability of at least one false rejection among m true-null tests: 1 - (1 - alpha)^m for independent tests.

concepts.title: Bonferroni correction
concepts.summary: Test each of m comparisons at alpha / m to keep the family-wise rate at or below alpha.

concepts.title: Least-squares line
concepts.summary: The line that minimises the sum of squared vertical gaps; slope = Sxy/Sxx and it passes through (x-bar, y-bar).

concepts.title: Residual
concepts.summary: Observed y minus the line's predicted y.

concepts.title: Random assignment
concepts.summary: Allocating units to arms by chance so that, on average, known and unknown traits balance.

concepts.title: Randomisation test
concepts.summary: Reassign labels in every possible way and count how often the difference is as large as the observed one.

concepts.title: Confounder
concepts.summary: A factor that influences both the exposure and the outcome and so creates a spurious or distorted association.

concepts.title: Simpson's paradox
concepts.summary: A comparison that holds in every subgroup can reverse in the pooled data when group sizes differ across arms.

concepts.title: Causal diagram
concepts.summary: A directed acyclic graph whose arrows mean 'directly influences'.

concepts.title: Collider
concepts.summary: A variable with two arrows pointing into it; conditioning on it opens a path that was blocked.

concepts.title: Difference in differences
concepts.summary: The change in the treated group minus the change in a comparison group over the same period.

concepts.title: Parallel trends
concepts.summary: The assumption that, without treatment, both groups would have changed by the same amount.

steps.headline: Listing every possible sample shows that a sample mean has a distribution of its own.

lead.text: Take a population of just three values, 2, 4 and 6, and draw two of them at random, putting the first back before drawing the second. That gives 3 × 3 = 9 equally likely ordered samples, and each has a mean: (2, 2) averages to 2, (2, 4) to 3, (2, 6) to 4, and so on up to (6, 6) at 6.

The figure begins with the population, whose mean is 4, and lets you move to the nine samples and then to their nine means. Those nine numbers, with the chance of each, are called the **sampling distribution** of the mean for samples of size 2: the distribution of a statistic over *every* sample of that size that could be drawn.

afterFigure.text: In practice you see only one of the nine, never all of them, so the sampling distribution describes the draws you did not make. That is what lets us say how far the one we did see is likely to have strayed from the truth.

steps.headline: The means of samples are less spread out than the values they are made from.

lead.text: The nine means average exactly 4, the population mean, so the sample mean is neither high nor low on the whole. Its spread is another matter. The population values 2, 4 and 6 have a variance of 8/3, about 2.67, because their squared distances from 4 are 4, 0 and 4. The nine means have squared distances 4, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1 and 4, which add to 12, and 12/9 = 4/3, about 1.33.

So the variance of the means is *exactly half* the variance of the data, and half is 1/2, the reciprocal of the sample size. Averaging two values lets a high draw and a low draw cancel, which a single draw never can.

steps.headline: The standard error of a mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n.

lead.text: The check we have just made generalises. For samples of size n, the variance of the sample mean is the population variance divided by n, and the standard deviation of the sample mean is the square root of that, which is called the **standard error**:
SE = sd / √n.

For the population {2, 4, 6}, sd = √(8/3) ≈ 1.633, and with n = 2 the standard error is 1.633 / 1.414 ≈ 1.155, which is the square root of the 4/3 found from the nine means. The formula agrees with the list.

The [[standard deviation|How far values typically sit from their mean. Met in Probability and Statistics.]] of the data measures how much *individual values* vary. The standard error measures how much *a sample mean* varies, and it is smaller for any n above 1.

steps.headline: Find the standard error of the mean when the sd is 12 and n = 36.

workedSteps.text: Write the formula with the numbers in place.
The square root of 36 is 6. Why is the sd divided by this root and not by 36 itself?
Divide.

steps.headline: Keep the sd at 12 and raise n to 144.

workedSteps.text: The square root of 144 is 12.
Work out the standard error.

steps.headline: Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error.

lead.text: The two answers just found, 2 and 1, differ by a factor of two, but n went from 36 to 144, a factor of four. That is the square root at work: to halve the error, the root of n must double, so n must be multiplied by 2 × 2 = 4. Doubling n alone divides the error by only √2, about 1.41.

The curve in the figure falls quickly at first and then flattens. Going from n = 4 to n = 16 cuts the error from 6 to 3, whereas going from n = 100 to n = 160 gains very little, so each extra observation buys less than the one before.
The same rule runs backwards, which is how a study is planned. To reach a target standard error, solve for n: n = (sd / SE)². With sd 12 and a target of 1.5, n = (12 / 1.5)² = 64.

steps.headline: The standard error depends on n and the spread, and not on the size of the population.

lead.text: Two misreadings are common. The first treats the standard error as the spread of the data; it is the spread of the *estimate*, and the division by √n is exactly what separates them. A table that prints only "sd" can hide which of the two it means, so check whether n has been divided out.

The second assumes a bigger population needs a proportionally bigger sample. The formula contains the sd and n and nothing else, so a sample of 100 gives the same standard error in a town as in a country, provided the sample is a small fraction of the population. That condition fails only when you sample a large share of a small population.

reveal.text: The formula contains no population size, so the two polls are equally precise, which is why national polls of about a thousand people can work.

lessons.orientation: Compute the standard error of a mean and say how sample size changes it.

blocks.text: A sample mean is one result out of many that the sampling could have produced. Draw two values at random from a population of 2, 4 and 6, putting the first back before the second, and the mean might come out as 2, as 6 or as anything between, so a second pair would very likely give a different answer. How far these answers vary from one sample to the next is measured by the **standard error**, the standard deviation of the sample mean.

That spread decides how far an estimate can be trusted, since a mean that could easily have come out quite differently says little about the population behind it, and it decides how much data a study needs before its estimate is useful. Both questions have a short formula as their answer, and a population of three values has only nine possible samples, so the formula can be checked against a complete list.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the standard error of a mean, and say how large a sample must be to reach a target error.
intro.whyItMatters: A single estimate says little until you know how much it would change on a repeat sample.

recap.keyIdea: The standard error of a mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n, so quadrupling the sample halves it.

blocks.text: Every possible sample of a given size has a mean, and those means form the sampling distribution. For the nine samples from {2, 4, 6} the means centre on 4 and have half the population variance, which is the square root rule seen in miniature.
The standard error, sd / √n, is the spread of the estimate and not of the data. It falls only with the square root of n and does not depend on the size of the population.

lessons.title: Areas under the normal curve

reveal.text: The exact value is 2.28 percent, slightly smaller than the rounded rule suggests, and a later screen shows where the exact number comes from.

steps.headline: A z-score counts how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean, and that one number turns any normal problem into the same curve.

lead.text: Adult heights in a population have a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm. A person of 186 cm is 16 cm above the mean, but 16 cm means little until it is compared with the spread, and 16 is exactly two standard deviations of 8. Dividing the distance from the mean by the standard deviation gives **z = (x − mean) / sd**, called the **z-score**, so for 186 cm it is (186 − 170) / 8 = 2.

The figure draws the same curve on two axes, centimetres above and z-scores below. Because z has no units, a z-score of 2 means the same thing for heights, exam marks or the weight of bolts, and one table of areas under a single curve, the standard normal, can answer every question about every normal distribution.

afterFigure.text: A person at z = 2 is taller than all but about 2.28 percent of the population, a figure we will meet properly in a few screens.

diagram.alt: A bell curve of heights with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. A raw axis in centimetres from 146 to 194 sits above a z axis from -3 to 3. The tail beyond 186 cm, which is z = 2, is shaded and holds about 2.28 percent of the area.
diagram.caption: The same curve read in centimetres and in z-scores. 186 cm lies two standard deviations above the mean.

Any value can be turned into a z-score, which is what allows different measurements to be compared on the same scale.

steps.headline: On a normal curve a share of the population is an area, and three areas are worth knowing by heart.

lead.text: The height of the curve is not a probability. What the curve gives is a share of the population for any stretch of the axis, which is the *area* under it above that stretch, and the area under the whole curve is 1. A single value has no width and so area zero, which is why we always ask about a range.

Take test scores with mean 100 and sd 15. The band from 85 to 115, one standard deviation either side of the mean, holds about **68 percent** of the area. Two standard deviations either side, from 70 to 130, hold about **95 percent**, and three, from 55 to 145, hold about **99.7 percent**. The figure lets you widen the band.

afterFigure.text: Everything outside three standard deviations is rare enough that a value out there deserves a second look.

diagram.alt: Three views of a bell curve of scores with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. The area within one standard deviation, 85 to 115, is about 68 percent, within two, 70 to 130, about 95 percent, and within three, 55 to 145, about 99.7 percent.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to widen the shaded band from one to three standard deviations.

steps.headline: Tables give the exact area below any z, and 1.96 is the value that leaves 2.5 percent in each tail.

lead.text: The rough 68, 95 and 99.7 are enough for a first impression, but exact work uses a table or a calculator that gives the area *below* a chosen z. For z = 2 the area below is 0.9772, so the area above is 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228, the 2.28 percent from the heights example.

One value is used so often that it is worth remembering: **z = 1.96**, which leaves 0.025 in each tail and therefore 0.95 in the middle. The "95 percent within two standard deviations" is the rounded version of it, and later lessons use 1.96 for every interval and test at the 95 percent level.

Why do we need this curve at all? In the first lesson the sample mean had a spread of its own, the standard error, and for a reasonably large sample the sample means pile up in a bell shape around the true mean. The same table then applies to them, with z = (sample mean − true mean) / SE.

afterFigure.text: The curve is a model, and it fits only when the data, or for a large sample the sample mean, are roughly bell-shaped. Incomes and waiting times are skewed, and for them the normal areas mislead.

lead.text: Two readings of these numbers go wrong often enough to name. The first treats z = 2 as "2 percent". It is a distance in standard deviations, and the share beyond it is about 2.3 percent only because of how the bell curve is shaped. A z of 1 leaves 16 percent beyond it, and a z of 3 leaves 0.13 percent.

The second is to apply the areas to anything. If the data are strongly skewed, the share beyond z = 2 can be very different from 2.3 percent. The normal areas are safe for the *sample mean* of a large sample, because of the pattern the first lesson began to show, and are unsafe for individual values from a skewed population.

blocks.text: A person who is 186 cm tall, in a population whose mean height is 170 cm and whose standard deviation is 8 cm, stands 16 cm above the mean, and that distance means little until it is set beside the spread. Measured in units of 8 cm it is exactly 2, which is also how far a score of 130 lies above the mean of 100 on a test with a standard deviation of 15, so counting distances in standard deviations lets quantities in different units be compared directly.

On that scale a single bell-shaped curve, the normal curve, gives the share of a population beyond any distance from the mean, and it does so for every normal distribution at once. That share answers the question of how unusual a value is, and it answers it equally for a sample mean once its distance from the truth is counted in standard errors.

recap.keyIdea: A z-score counts distance from the mean in standard deviations, and the share of a normal distribution beyond it is an area under the standard curve.

blocks.text: Subtracting the mean and dividing by the sd turns any normal value into a z-score, so that a single curve and a single table cover them all. Within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations lie about 68, 95 and 99.7 percent, and z = 1.96 leaves 2.5 percent in each tail.
The area above a value is 1 minus the area below it, and the areas apply to a sample mean through its standard error, provided the sample is large enough for its means to be bell-shaped.

lessons.title: An interval for a mean

steps.headline: A confidence interval is the sample mean plus and minus a margin of error built from the standard error.

lead.text: A study of 36 people gives a sample mean of 52, and suppose the population sd is known to be 9. The standard error is 9 / √36 = 1.5, and from the last lesson, 95 percent of sample means land within 1.96 standard errors of the true mean. Turning that around, the true mean is very likely within 1.96 standard errors of the sample mean we got.

That gives the construction: **estimate ± critical value × SE**. The multiplier 1.96 is the **critical value** for 95 percent, and the product 1.96 × 1.5 = 2.94 is the **margin of error**, the half-width of the interval. The interval runs from 52 − 2.94 = 49.06 to 52 + 2.94 = 54.94, and we write it (49.06, 54.94). The figure shows it with the 90, 95 and 99 percent versions.

afterFigure.text: The interval is about the true *mean*. It does not say where individual people lie, a point we return to shortly.

steps.headline: The interval narrows with a bigger sample and widens with more spread or a higher confidence level.

lead.text: Each of the three pieces of the margin can be changed. A larger n shrinks the standard error, so the interval narrows, and by the square root rule it needs four times the data to halve it. A larger sd widens it. A higher confidence level swaps 1.96 for a bigger multiplier, 2.576 at 99 percent in place of 1.645 at 90 percent, and so widens it too.

The last of these is the easy one to get backwards. Higher confidence feels like a better result, but it is bought with width, and an interval that is 99 percent sure of covering the mean is a *less precise* statement than one that is only 90 percent sure.

afterFigure.text: The only way to gain both confidence and precision is more data.

steps.headline: When sigma is estimated from the sample, the multiplier comes from the t distribution and is larger than 1.96.

lead.text: In real studies the population sd is rarely known, and the sample sd, s, stands in for it. That adds a second source of error, since s is itself a wobbling estimate, especially from a small sample. The multiplier has to grow to allow for it, and the table that supplies it is the **t distribution**, indexed by the **degrees of freedom**, which for a mean is n − 1.

The curve in the figure shows how the 95 percent multiplier depends on them. With 15 degrees of freedom it is 2.131, with 5 it is 2.571, and by 30 it is 2.042, close to 1.96. For a large sample the two multipliers are almost the same, and for a small one using 1.96 would give an interval that is too narrow.

afterFigure.text: Only the multiplier changes. The rest of the construction is as before, with s in place of sigma in the standard error.

steps.headline: An interval describes the mean and not individuals, and the sentence reporting it should claim no more than that.

lead.text: A confidence interval of (49.06, 54.94) does not say that 95 percent of the individual values fall between 49.06 and 54.94. It concerns the *mean*. With sd 9, individual values are spread over roughly 52 ± 1.96 × 9, which is 34.36 to 69.64, a range more than six times as wide.

A fair report gives the interval with its units and level: "the mean was 52 (95 percent interval 49.06 to 54.94)". It does not say that the mean is certainly inside, and it should not be read as covering the people measured. The next lesson looks at exactly what the 95 percent promises.

reveal.text: The interval for the mean is narrow because 9 observations average out. Individual values are not averaged, so they spread far more widely.

lessons.orientation: Build a confidence interval for a mean and say what widens or narrows it.
lessons.nextAction: Next you will see what the 95 percent in an interval actually promises, by drawing many intervals and counting how many cover the true mean.

blocks.text: A study of 36 people reports a sample mean of 52 with a standard error of 1.5, and the natural next step is to say where the true mean of the population lies. A sample mean cannot settle that exactly, because a different 36 people would give a different mean, but the spread of the sample mean is known: 95 percent of sample means land within 1.96 standard errors of the truth.

That statement starts from the true mean and describes where the sample falls, whereas what you hold is the sample and what you want is a statement about the truth. Turning it around gives a range of true means that are consistent with the sample, called a **confidence interval**, and it is how an estimate is reported together with an honest account of its uncertainty.

intro.whyItMatters: An estimate with no interval does not say whether a result is solid or a fluke of the sample.

recap.keyIdea: A confidence interval is the sample mean plus and minus a critical value times the standard error, using t when sigma has to be estimated.

blocks.text: The margin of error is the critical value times the standard error. A bigger sample narrows the interval by the square root rule, more spread widens it, and a higher confidence level widens it by raising the critical value.
With sigma estimated by s and a small n, the multiplier comes from the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, and the interval describes the mean and not the individual values.

lessons.title: What 95 percent promises

reveal.text: Twenty intervals with a miss rate of 5 percent give one miss on average, although a particular set of twenty can easily have none, or two.

steps.headline: Drawing many intervals from the same population shows that a few of them miss the true mean.

lead.text: Take a population whose true mean is 50 and whose sd is 10, and draw a sample of 25. Its standard error is 10 / 5 = 2, so a 95 percent interval is the sample mean plus and minus 1.96 × 2 = 3.92. Draw another sample and you get another interval, centred somewhere else. The figure shows twenty such intervals against the true mean, which is held fixed at 50.

Most of the bars cross the dashed line, and the ones that miss are drawn in red. The first set has one miss. The second set, from a fresh set of twenty samples, has two. The true value never moved; the *intervals* did.

afterFigure.text: This is the picture behind the phrase "95 percent confidence", and it is a statement about many repeated samples.

steps.headline: The 95 percent describes the method over many samples and not the one interval you have in hand.

lead.text: Once a single interval has been computed, the true mean is a fixed number and the interval is a fixed pair of numbers, so the interval either contains the mean or it does not. There is no chance left in the matter. The 95 percent describes the **procedure**: the share of intervals produced by this method that cover the truth, across repeated samples. This is the meaning of **confidence level**.

It is tempting to say there is a 95 percent chance the true mean lies inside this interval, and that statement quietly changes what the 95 percent refers to. A better sentence is "this interval comes from a method that captures the truth 95 percent of the time". A miss is also less surprising than it seems. The chance that all of ten independent intervals cover is 0.95^10 = 0.599, so even a set of only ten has about a 40 percent chance of containing *at least one* miss.

reveal.text: Less than a 36 percent chance of an unbroken run is the reason you should not be shocked to find one miss in twenty.

steps.headline: An interval for a proportion uses the same construction, with the standard error built from the proportion itself.

lead.text: A poll asks 120 people about a plan and 42 support it, so the sample proportion is p̂ = 42 / 120 = 0.35. The standard error of a **proportion** is √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n), and here it is √(0.35 × 0.65 / 120) = 0.0435. The margin of error at 95 percent is 1.96 × 0.0435 = 0.0853, and the interval runs from 0.265 to 0.435.

The shape is the one from the last lesson: estimate ± critical value × SE. The second view in the figure multiplies the poll by ten, to 420 of 1200, and shows the same proportion with a margin of 0.027, about a third as wide.

afterFigure.text: The formula is an approximation and needs at least 10 successes and 10 failures in the sample.

steps.headline: Every value inside the interval is plausible, and the formula should be used only when there are enough successes and failures.

lead.text: A poll that reports 52 percent with a margin of 3 points is not saying that the truth is 52 percent. The whole interval, 49 to 55 percent, is a set of plausible values, and the centre is only the single best guess. If the interval includes 50 percent, as it does here, the poll cannot tell you whether a majority supports the plan.

The formula also fails for tiny counts. With 4 supporters in 50 people, or 1 in 12, the bell-shaped approximation behind it does not hold, and the interval can mislead. A common rule asks for at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

lessons.orientation: Interpret a confidence level as a property of the method and build an interval for a proportion.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson starts testing claims, by asking how surprising a sample would be if a claim about the mean were true.

blocks.text: A 95 percent confidence interval is usually read as a 95 percent chance that the true mean lies inside it, since "we are 95 percent confident" seems to say just that. The true mean is a fixed number, though, and if twenty samples of 25 are drawn from a population whose mean is 50, each sample gives a different interval while 50 stays where it is, so the 95 percent cannot describe the true value moving in and out of the intervals.

What it describes is the method: across many samples, about 95 percent of the intervals it produces cover the true mean. That is the reading that lets you judge any reported interval, whether it is the margin of error on a poll or the interval around a mean, for what it supports and what it does not.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a 95 percent confidence level promises, and build an interval for a proportion from a poll.
intro.whyItMatters: Reading the 95 percent as a probability about one interval is the commonest misreading of any study.

recap.keyIdea: A 95 percent confidence level describes the method over repeated samples, and an interval for a proportion has the same shape as one for a mean.

blocks.text: Across repeated samples a 95 percent method covers the true value 95 percent of the time, and misses about 1 in 20, but a single computed interval either contains it or does not. The interval for a proportion is p̂ ± 1.96 × √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n), valid when there are at least 10 successes and 10 failures.
Every value inside the interval is plausible, and the centre has no special standing.

lessons.title: How surprising is this sample?

steps.headline: A test starts from a claim about the mean and asks how far the sample mean lies from it, counted in standard errors.

lead.text: A scale of test scores is claimed to have a mean of 100, with a known sigma of 15. A sample of 36 people has a mean of 104. Is that evidence against the claim, or the sort of thing that sampling alone produces? The claim being examined is the **null hypothesis**, here "the true mean is 100", and a test works by *assuming it is true* and seeing whether the data would then be surprising.

The standard error is 15 / √36 = 2.5, so the sample mean lies 4 / 2.5 = 1.6 standard errors above the claimed mean. This distance is the **test statistic**, **z = (sample mean − claimed mean) / SE**, and it is the same standardising step as in the second lesson. A z of 1.6 says how far, and the next question is how often chance alone would reach that far.

reveal.text: The null is usually a statement of no effect or no difference, and a test tries to see whether the data are too surprising to keep believing it.
A z of 1.5 is a moderate distance from the claim, in the range where chance alone often reaches.
About 5.5 percent of samples would, and that probability is the first step towards the p-value.

steps.headline: The p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a sample at least as far from it as the one we have.

lead.text: The figure shows the **sampling distribution** of the mean if the null were true, centred on 100 with standard error 2.5, and marks the observed mean 104. The area above 104 is 0.0548. A mean at least as far from 100 in the *other* direction would have been just as surprising, so a two-sided test also counts the area below 96, and the total is 0.1096.

That total is the **p-value**: the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is calculated entirely inside the world where the null is true, which is why it cannot be the probability that the null *is* true.

afterFigure.text: A small p-value means the data would be rare if the null were true. A large one means they would be unremarkable.

steps.headline: A p-value above 0.05 does not prove there is no effect, and a small one does not show a large one.

lead.text: The threshold is a decision rule agreed before the data are seen, commonly 0.05, and a p-value below it is called *statistically significant*. With p = 0.1096 the scores study does not reach it, but this means only that the data were not surprising enough. It does not mean the mean is 100, and a larger sample might well have shown a difference.

The opposite error is to read a small p-value as a large effect. The figure compares two studies against the same claim. The first has a difference of 4 points from 36 people and p = 0.110. The second has a difference of only 0.5 points, but from 3600 people, so its standard error is 0.25, z = 2 and p = 0.046. The smaller effect is the more surprising one, because *surprise depends on the standard error as well as on the difference*.
Report the p-value itself with an interval for the size of the effect, and never treat the 0.05 line as a switch between true and false.

reveal.text: A p-value this small does not make a difference of under one point important. How much it matters is a question about the subject, which the p-value cannot answer.

lessons.orientation: Carry out a test of a mean and read a p-value without overstating it.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson names the two ways a test can go wrong and shows how the threshold trades one against the other.

blocks.text: A scale of test scores is said to have a mean of 100, and a sample of 36 people gives a mean of 104. The gap of 4 points could be a real difference, or it could be the ordinary wobble of a sample mean, and the standard error is the yardstick that separates the two: with a standard deviation of 15 it is 15 / 6 = 2.5, so the sample mean lies 1.6 standard errors from the claim.

Whether 1.6 standard errors is far enough to doubt the claim depends on how often chance alone would stray that far, and that frequency can be worked out by assuming the claim is true and asking how the sample means would then be spread. Reported as a single number, the **p-value**, it accompanies nearly every published result, and it is easy to misread.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to run a test of a mean, find a two-sided p-value and say what it does and does not mean.
intro.whyItMatters: Nearly every published result is accompanied by a p-value, and nearly every one is misread.

recap.keyIdea: A p-value is the chance, if the null hypothesis were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one seen, and it measures surprise and not size.

blocks.text: A test sets a null hypothesis, standardises the sample mean to z = (sample mean − claimed mean) / SE, and converts z to a tail area, doubled for a two-sided test. The result is the probability of data this extreme if the null were true.
It is not the probability that the null is true, a value above 0.05 does not prove no effect, and a small value can come from a tiny effect in a very large sample.

lessons.title: Two ways to be wrong

steps.headline: A test run on data where nothing is going on still rejects about alpha of the time, and each such rejection is a false alarm.

lead.text: Run a test at the 0.05 level on 1000 data sets in which the null hypothesis is true. The p-values from such data are spread evenly, so about 5 percent of them, around 50, land below 0.05 and the test rejects. In one such run of 1000 it rejected 48 times, a rate of 48 / 1000 = 0.048.

Rejecting a null that is true is called a **Type I error**, and the probability of it is the threshold itself, **alpha**. It is fixed *before* the data are seen, and it describes how often the procedure raises a false alarm when nothing is there. It is not the probability that a rejected null is true, a figure that also depends on how often real effects exist.

reveal.text: Alpha is the chance of a Type I error when the null is true, which is why 0.05 gives roughly 1 false alarm in 20.

steps.headline: When a real effect exists the test can still fail to reject, and the share of real effects it does catch is the power.

lead.text: Now run the test on data sets in which a real effect is present. Not every run will reject, because a sample can fall on the unlucky side of the cut-off. In 200 runs with a real effect, 70 failed to reject, so 130 of 200 caught it. Failing to reject a null that is false is a **Type II error**, its probability is **beta**, and the share of real effects the test catches, 1 − beta, is its **power**.

The figure puts the two kinds of run side by side. The false-alarm rate is 0.048, close to the planned 0.05. The power is 130 / 200 = 0.65, so the test missed a real effect in more than a third of runs.

steps.headline: Moving the cut-off trades one error for the other, and only more data lowers both.

lead.text: The figure draws two curves of the test statistic: one for data where the claim is true, centred on 0, and a dashed one for data with a real effect, centred on 2.5 standard errors away. The test rejects beyond a cut-off. The part of the first curve outside the cut-off is alpha. The part of the second inside the cut-off is beta.

Move the cut-off outwards, from 1.96 to 2.576, and alpha shrinks from 0.050 to 0.010, but beta grows from 0.295 to 0.530, and the power falls from 0.705 to 0.470. Moving it inward does the opposite. So a lower alpha is not free safety: with the sample fixed it buys fewer false alarms at the price of more missed effects.
There is one way to lower both, which is more data. A larger sample narrows both curves, so they separate, and the cut-off can sit between them with little area on the wrong side.

steps.headline: Failing to reject a null does not make it true, and alpha is not the chance that a rejected null is true.

lead.text: Two readings of these rates go wrong most often. The first treats a failure to reject as evidence that the null is true. If the test had low power, a miss is common even when an effect is real, so "no significant difference" from a small study says little. It says only that the study could not tell.

The second reads alpha as the probability that the null is true given that we rejected. Alpha is the rate of rejection *when the null is true*. The two conditional probabilities are different numbers, and the second depends on how many of the nulls tested were true in the first place, which a later lesson returns to.

reveal.text: A study that could only catch a real effect 30 percent of the time has not shown that there is nothing to find.

blocks.text: Run a test at the 0.05 level on 1000 data sets in which nothing is going on, and about 50 of them will be declared significant. The test is behaving as designed, and yet each of those 50 results is an effect found where none exists. Run the same test on data in which a real effect is present and it will sometimes fail the other way, because a sample can land on the wrong side of the cut-off and the effect goes unnoticed.

A test can therefore be wrong in two different ways, each with its own rate, and with a fixed sample, moving the threshold lowers one rate only by raising the other. Knowing both rates, and being able to estimate them by counting the runs of a test, is what lets you say how much weight a single verdict from a test deserves.

intro.whyItMatters: A result called significant, and a result called not significant, can each be wrong, in different ways and at different rates.

recap.keyIdea: A test can reject a true null, at rate alpha, or miss a real effect, at rate beta, and lowering alpha with a fixed sample raises beta.

blocks.text: Rejecting a true null is a Type I error with probability alpha, and failing to reject a false one is a Type II error with probability beta, so that power is 1 minus beta. Both can be estimated by running the test many times and counting.
Moving the cut-off trades one error for the other, and only a larger sample reduces both. A failure to reject from a low-power study does not show that the null is true.

lessons.title: How big should the study be?

steps.headline: A study should name, before it starts, the smallest effect it would matter to find.

lead.text: Suppose a programme is meant to raise a test score, and scores have a standard deviation of 10. A rise of 1 point would not change anything for anyone, whereas a rise of 5 points would, so 5 is the smallest effect worth detecting, and the whole design should be built around catching it. That number is the **effect size**, and in units of the sd it is 5 / 10 = 0.5.

Choosing it comes first, and it comes from knowledge of the subject rather than from the data. A study planned *after* its results are known is chasing whatever it found, and one planned without any effect in mind cannot say how many people are enough.

steps.headline: Power is the chance the test statistic lands beyond the cut-off when the real effect is present, and it comes from the effect, the spread and n.

lead.text: Take a real effect of 5 with sd 10 and n = 25. The standard error is 10 / 5 = 2, so the sample mean would typically sit 5 / 2 = 2.5 standard errors from zero. A two-sided test at 0.05 rejects when z passes 1.96 in either direction. The chance that a statistic centred on 2.5 passes 1.96 is the area to the right of 1.96 on the dashed curve in the figure, which is Φ(2.5 − 1.96) = Φ(0.54) = 0.705, where Φ(z) is the table's area below z under the standard normal curve. The chance of passing −1.96 on the far side is Φ(−2.5 − 1.96) = 0.000004, and is added for completeness.

So this study has a power of about **0.705**: it would catch the effect in 70 percent of repetitions, and miss it in 30 percent. The figure lets you raise n to 32 and 64 and watch the dashed curve move across the cut-off.

afterFigure.text: Everything here uses the normal model with the standard deviation taken as known, which is a good approximation for studies of this size.

steps.headline: To plan a study, turn the power calculation around and solve for n.

lead.text: Power depends on four things: the effect, the spread, n and alpha. Raising n or the effect, or lowering the spread, raises it, and so does a looser alpha at the cost of more false alarms. Usually the effect, the spread and alpha are fixed by the problem, and the quantity we choose is n. By convention the target is **80 percent power**.

Ignoring the negligible far tail, 80 percent power needs the real effect to sit 1.96 + 0.8416 = 2.8016 standard errors from zero, where 0.8416 is the z value that leaves 80 percent of a normal curve below it. Setting 2.8016 = effect / (sd / √n) and solving gives **n = ((1.96 + 0.8416) × sd / effect)²**. For effect 5 and sd 10 this is (2.8016 × 2)² = 31.4, and the sample size is rounded *up* to 32, because 31 would fall just short.
Check it against the power figure earlier in the lesson, where n = 32 gave a power of 0.807, just above 0.80.

steps.headline: A study with too little power cannot say much when it finds nothing, and one that finds something may exaggerate it.

lead.text: A study that is too small to catch the effect it is looking for will usually return "not significant", which is easy to read as "no effect" and is nothing of the kind. At a power of 0.3 it misses a real effect 70 percent of the time. Such a study can still produce a significant result by luck, and when it does the estimate tends to be too large, because only the unusually large estimates pass the cut-off.

The remedy is to settle the smallest effect that matters, the spread (from a pilot or earlier work) and the power wanted, and to compute n before collecting data. Doing it afterwards, from the effect that was observed, only repeats the p-value.

reveal.text: The sample grows with the inverse square of the effect, so detecting half the effect costs four times the people.

blocks.text: A study of 25 people looks for an improvement of 5 points on a scale with a standard deviation of 10. The standard error of its mean is 2, so a real improvement of 5 would put the sample mean 2.5 standard errors from zero, and a test at the 0.05 level rejects only when the mean ends up more than 1.96 standard errors out. A sample mean scatters around the real effect, so it will sometimes fall short of that cut-off, and about three studies in ten like this one would miss an effect that is really there.

How often a planned study catches the effect it is looking for is its power, and it depends on the size of the effect, the spread of the measurements and the number of people. That dependence can be worked out before any data are collected, which lets a study be sized beforehand to find the smallest effect that matters.

intro.whyItMatters: A study that is too small wastes the people in it, because it cannot tell a real effect from noise.

recap.keyIdea: Power depends on the effect, the spread, n and alpha, and the sample size for 80 percent power is ((1.96 + 0.8416) × sd / effect)², rounded up.

blocks.text: A study's power is the chance that its statistic passes the cut-off when the real effect is present, and it rises with n and effect and falls with spread. For an effect of 5 and an sd of 10, n = 25 gives 0.705 and n = 32 gives 0.807.

lessons.title: Compare two groups

steps.headline: The standard error of a difference is the square root of the sum of the two squared standard errors.

lead.text: Group A has 40 people with a mean of 82 and an sd of 10. Group B has 50 people with a mean of 76 and an sd of 12. The difference is 6, and, as always, it needs a standard error before we can say how far to trust it. Each mean has one of its own: 10 / √40 = 1.58 for A and 12 / √50 = 1.70 for B.

The two errors do not simply add, because the groups are independent and a high draw in one can be offset by a low draw in the other. What adds is the *variance* of each mean, so **SE(difference) = √(SE₁² + SE₂²)**. Here that is √(100/40 + 144/50) = √(2.5 + 2.88) = √5.38 = 2.32, smaller than the 3.28 that adding the two standard errors would give.

reveal.text: The standard error of the difference is larger than that of either mean alone, and smaller than their sum.

steps.headline: An interval for a difference that excludes zero is evidence of a real difference, and it is a better check than comparing two separate intervals.

lead.text: With SE = 2.32 the margin of error at 95 percent is 1.96 × 2.32 = 4.55, and the interval for the difference is 6 ± 4.55, or (1.45, 10.55). Zero is not in it, so a difference of no size at all is not a plausible value, and the data support a real difference in the same sense that a test at the 0.05 level would.

It is tempting to compare the intervals of the two groups instead. A runs from 78.90 to 85.10 and B from 72.67 to 79.33, and these overlap a little, which sounds like "no clear difference". The first figure shows the overlap, and the second shows that the interval for the difference does not include zero. Two intervals can overlap and the difference between the means can still be clear, because the standard error of a difference is smaller than the sum of the two margins.

afterFigure.text: Overlap of the two separate intervals is therefore a weaker test than the interval for the difference.

steps.headline: When the same people are measured twice, take the difference for each person and analyse the changes as one sample.

lead.text: People differ from one another a great deal, but a given person changes much less. Measuring the same four people before and after, 10, 12, 9, 14 and then 8, 11, 9, 11, the individual changes are −2, −1, 0 and −3. Their mean is −1.5, their sd is 1.29, and the standard error of the mean change is 1.29 / √4 = 0.645. This is a **paired** analysis, and from here it is an interval for one mean, using the t multiplier with 3 degrees of freedom, 3.182.

The margin is 3.182 × 0.645 = 2.05, and the interval is (−3.55, 0.55). It includes zero, so four people cannot settle whether there was any change. Had the same eight numbers been treated as two independent groups, the standard error would have been 1.34, more than twice as large, because the large differences *between* people would have been counted as noise.

afterFigure.text: The pairing removes the variation between people, which is usually the biggest part of the noise.

steps.headline: Pair only when each value in one group is matched to a value in the other, and never pair groups of different people.

lead.text: Pairing is justified by the *design* of the study, not by the look of the numbers. The same patients before and after, the two eyes of one person, or twins split between two treatments, all give natural pairs. Two groups of unrelated people do not, however similar their sizes, and treating them as pairs would invent a match that is not there.

The opposite mistake is also common. Analysing paired data as two independent groups throws away the match and usually widens the interval, as it did above. If the design pairs, the analysis should too.

reveal.text: An interval that lies wholly below zero shows a fall, which the four-person study above was too small to show.

lessons.orientation: Build an interval for a difference of means and decide when to pair the data.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson shows what happens to a p-value when a researcher runs many tests and reports the best one.

blocks.text: Group A has a mean of 82 and group B a mean of 76, and the difference of 6 between them is itself an estimate with an uncertainty of its own. That uncertainty is built from the standard errors of the two means and comes out smaller than their sum, because a high draw in one group and a low draw in the other partly cancel in the difference.

Once the difference has its own standard error, an interval and a test for it follow as they do for a single mean, and they answer the question that most studies are asking, which is whether two groups differ. The same numbers can also come from two groups or from one group measured twice, and which of the two it is changes the standard error a great deal.

intro.whyItMatters: Most comparisons in practice are between two groups, and the standard error of a difference is where they usually go wrong.

recap.keyIdea: The standard error of a difference is the square root of the sum of the squared standard errors, and paired data are analysed through their changes.

blocks.text: For independent groups the variances of the two means add, so SE = √(SE₁² + SE₂²), and the interval for the difference, not the overlap of two separate intervals, shows whether zero is plausible.
When the same people are measured twice, taking each person's change turns the data into a single sample, which usually gives a smaller standard error than treating the two columns as independent.

lessons.title: Many tests, one lucky result

steps.headline: Each test is a small risk, and a run of tests makes at least one false alarm likely.

lead.text: A test at the 0.05 level has a 1-in-20 chance of a false alarm when the null is true. Run 20 tests on 20 true nulls and you have 20 chances at a 1-in-20 event. The chance that *none* of the 20 raises a false alarm is 0.95 multiplied by itself 20 times, which is 0.358, so the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.358 = **0.642**.

The curve in the figure gives the general rule: with m independent tests the chance of at least one false rejection is **1 − 0.95^m**. It is 0.226 for 5 tests, 0.401 for 10, and 0.923 for 50. This chance of at least one false alarm across a set of tests is called the **family-wise error rate**.

afterFigure.text: Each of the individual tests still has a false-alarm rate of 0.05. The risk that grows is the risk across the whole set.

The per-test threshold is 0.01, a fifth of 0.05, and a result that fails it is not a finding at the overall 0.05 level.

steps.headline: The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the number of tests, and it pays for safety with power.

lead.text: A simple remedy is to make each test harder to pass. With m tests, use the threshold alpha / m, so that for 20 tests at an overall 0.05 each must reach p below 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025. This is the **Bonferroni correction**, and it keeps the family-wise error rate at or below 0.05 however the tests are related.

The figure shows the p-values of 20 tests in which every null is true. At the ordinary threshold, two of them look significant, which is what the curve led us to expect. At 0.0025 none does. The cost comes from the sixth lesson: a stricter threshold means more missed effects, so a corrected test needs a larger sample to keep its power.

afterFigure.text: Bonferroni controls one error rate, the chance of any false alarm, and nothing else. It does not make the surviving findings true.

steps.headline: The number of tests is every comparison that could have been reported, including the ones that were quietly dropped.

lead.text: The most damaging version is the invisible one. A researcher measures an outcome in 30 subgroups, by age, region, sex and so on, finds that one of them has p = 0.02 and reports only that. This counts as one test only if one was planned. The honest count is 30, the chance of a p below 0.05 somewhere among 30 true nulls is 1 − 0.95^30 = 0.79, and a p of 0.02 is then unremarkable.

The same reasoning goes beyond a single study. Ioannidis argued in 2005 that when many hypotheses are tested and few are true, a large share of "significant" findings can be false. The size of that share depends on how many real effects exist and how much power the tests have, so it cannot be read off from a p-value.

reveal.text: Without the correction, a slice with p below 0.05 would turn up by chance about 79 times in 100, which is why the number of slices has to be reported and counted.

steps.headline: Honest reporting counts every test, ideally states the tests in advance, and does not assume that a correction proves a finding.

lead.text: Three habits protect against the problem. First, decide the comparisons *before* looking at the data and record them, which is called pre-registration. Second, report every test that was run, including the ones that came to nothing, so that a reader can count the family. Third, where many comparisons are unavoidable, correct for them and say so.

The American Statistical Association said in its 2016 statement on p-values that proper inference requires full reporting and transparency, for exactly this reason. A correction helps, but it controls one error rate and nothing more, so a finding that survives it still needs replication.

blocks.text: A test on a true null at the 0.05 level has a 1-in-20 chance of a false alarm, which is a small risk when one test is run and a different matter when twenty are. Twenty tests on twenty true nulls are twenty chances at a 1-in-20 event, and that is the situation of anyone who searches a dataset for a pattern by trying many comparisons.

The chance that at least one of those tests reports a finding is well above 1 in 20, and it grows with every comparison added, whether or not the extra comparisons are ever reported. Being able to compute that chance, and to correct for it, is what lets you read a significant result in the light of how it was found.

intro.whyItMatters: A single significant result means little until you know how many tests were run to find it.

recap.keyIdea: With m tests the chance of at least one false alarm is 1 − (1 − alpha)^m, and the Bonferroni correction divides alpha by m.

blocks.text: Twenty independent tests of true nulls at 0.05 have a 0.642 chance of at least one false alarm. Dividing alpha by the number of tests, here 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025, holds the family-wise rate at 0.05 and lowers each test's power.
The count must include every comparison that could have been reported, and a correction controls one error rate, not the truth of the findings.

steps.headline: The least-squares line is the one for which the squared vertical gaps between the points and the line add up to the smallest total.

lead.text: Take four points, (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 4) and (3, 8), and try to draw one straight line through the middle of them. Many lines look reasonable, so we need a rule for choosing. Measure the vertical gap between each point and the line, square it so that gaps above and below cannot cancel, and add the squares. The guess y = 2x leaves gaps of 1, 1, 0 and 2, whose squares add to 6.

The **least-squares line** is the one with the smallest such total, and for these points it is y = 0.7 + 2.2x, which brings the total down to 1.8. The squares in the figure are drawn with sides equal to the gaps, so that you can see the area being minimised.

steps.headline: The slope is the sum of products of deviations divided by the sum of squared deviations in x, and the line passes through the point of means.

lead.text: For the four points the mean of x is 1.5 and the mean of y is 4. The deviations in x are −1.5, −0.5, 0.5 and 1.5, and in y they are −3, −1, 0 and 4. Multiplying them in pairs and adding gives **Sxy** = 4.5 + 0.5 + 0 + 6 = 11, and squaring the x deviations and adding gives **Sxx** = 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5.

The slope is **Sxy / Sxx** = 11 / 5 = 2.2. The line always passes through the point (x̄, ȳ) = (1.5, 4), so its intercept is ȳ − slope × x̄ = 4 − 2.2 × 1.5 = 0.7. The slope reads as the change in y that goes with a one-unit change in x, *averaged over the points*.

reveal.text: The intercept is where the line crosses the y axis, and it is fixed as soon as the slope and the point of means are known.
The line says 7.3, and the gap to the observed 8 has a name, which is the subject of the next screen.

steps.headline: A residual is the gap between an observed value and the line, and the least-squares residuals always sum to zero.

lead.text: At x = 3 the line predicts 7.3 and the observed value is 8, so the point lies 0.7 above the line. This gap, observed minus predicted, is the **residual**. The four residuals for our line are 0.3, 0.1, −1.1 and 0.7, which sum to zero, and their squares, 0.09, 0.01, 1.21 and 0.49, sum to 1.8, the total of the squared gaps drawn at the start of the lesson.

How much of the scatter in y does the line account for? The share of the variation explained is called **R²**. For our four points the squared residuals add to 1.8, while the total variation of y about its mean of 4 is 9 + 1 + 0 + 16 = 26, so R² = 1 − 1.8 / 26 = 0.93.
An R² of 0.93 says the line accounts for 93 percent of the variation in these four points.

reveal.text: A residual of −0.8 says the point sits 0.8 below the line, whereas a point above the line has a positive residual.

Ask the same line about a 40-year-old and it answers 319.7 cm. steps.headline: A slope describes how two variables move together, and it does not say that changing one would change the other.

lead.text: The slope of 2.2 says that, across these four units, those with an x one unit higher tended to have a y 2.2 higher. It compares *different units* with each other. It does not say that raising x for any one unit would raise its y by 2.2, because the units with high x may differ from the others in other ways as well.

Cities with more ice cream sales have more drownings, so the fitted slope is positive, yet no one thinks ice cream causes drowning. Warm weather puts more people on the beach and more people in the water, and the line cannot tell the difference. The rest of the course is about when a difference can be read as a cause.

blocks.text: Four points, (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 4) and (3, 8), lie roughly along a rising line, yet no single straight line passes through all four. Some line has to be chosen to stand for them, and the rule used almost everywhere is to make the squared vertical gaps between the points and the line as small as they can be, which gives the **least-squares line**.

A line chosen this way sums up a relationship in two numbers, a slope and an intercept, and it lets you predict a value that was never measured. What the slope reports is how the points are arranged, and it is easy to read it as more than that, as a claim that changing x would change y.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a least-squares line, read a residual, and say when a fitted line should not be trusted.
intro.whyItMatters: A fitted line is the basic description of how two measurements move together, and it is where most claims of cause begin.

recap.keyIdea: The least-squares line minimises the squared vertical gaps, and its slope describes how two variables move together without showing that one causes the other.

blocks.text: The slope is Sxy / Sxx and the line passes through the point of means. A residual is the observed value minus the line's prediction, and the squared residuals add to the quantity the line minimises.
The line describes the range it was fitted on, and its slope compares different units rather than showing what would happen if one unit were changed.

lessons.title: Randomise to compare

steps.headline: When people choose their own treatment, a difference between the arms can come from who chose and not from the treatment.

lead.text: Suppose 200 people are offered a new drug, and the 100 who take it recover more often than the 100 who do not. One explanation is that the drug works. Another is that the people who chose it were the keen, motivated ones, who also follow their doctor's advice, rest and eat well. Their recovery would have differed even if the drug were an inert pill.

The first view in the figure shows the problem: 80 of the drug arm are keen and only 20 of the other arm. The arms differ in keenness before the drug does anything, and the comparison mixes the effect of the drug with the effect of that difference. The keenness is not recorded as a column in the data, so nothing can be adjusted for it afterwards.

steps.headline: Random assignment gives each person the same chance of either arm, so any trait, recorded or not, is spread evenly between the arms on average.

lead.text: The coin that decides the arm does not know who is keen, who is old, who is poor or who has a trait nobody thought to measure. Each person has the same chance of either arm whatever their traits, so every trait is balanced *on average* between the arms. A difference in outcome that is bigger than chance can then be put down to the treatment, because the treatment is the only thing the coin changed. This is **random assignment**.

It should not be confused with random sampling. Sampling people at random from a population lets you generalise to that population. Assigning them at random to arms lets you infer cause. Matching the arms on a few traits, such as age and sex, balances only those, and the unmeasured traits can still differ.
The balance holds on average and not in every trial. In a small trial the arms can differ by chance, which is why a p-value is still needed.

reveal.text: The control group and the treated group are made alike by the coin, and the treatment is all that separates them.

steps.headline: Blocking cuts the noise, and blinding cuts the bias.

lead.text: Two further devices belong with randomisation. **Blocking** sorts people into groups of similar people first, such as by age band, and randomises within each group, so that the arms are guaranteed to be alike on that trait and the comparison is less noisy. It is a way to improve precision, and the coin still decides inside each block.

**Blinding** hides the arm from the people involved. If participants do not know whether they received the drug, their expectation cannot shape how they feel or report, and if the people measuring the outcome do not know either, their expectation cannot shape the measurement. A trial in which neither group knows is called double-blind.

reveal.text: Blinding protects against expectation, whereas randomisation protects against differences between the arms that existed before treatment.

steps.headline: A randomisation test finds the p-value by counting how many of the equally likely assignments give a difference as large as the one seen.

lead.text: Take 6 people with outcomes 4, 6, 7, 11, 12 and 14, and let a coin choose 3 of them for treatment. There are 6 × 5 × 4 / (3 × 2 × 1) = 20 equally likely ways to choose the treated group. Suppose the three people actually treated are the three with outcomes 11, 12 and 14. The treated mean is 12.33, the control mean is 5.67, and the difference is 6.67.

If the treatment did nothing, the outcomes were fixed in advance and the coin merely decided who was labelled treated. The figure computes the difference for all 20 ways the labels could have fallen. Only one assignment, the actual one, gives a difference as large as 6.67, so the one-sided **randomisation p-value** is 1 / 20 = 0.05. Counting the mirror assignment as well, a two-sided test gives 2 / 20 = 0.10.

afterFigure.text: No normal curve was used. The p-value comes straight from counting the assignments the coin could have produced.

steps.headline: Randomisation does not guarantee equal groups, and it protects the comparison but not every other part of the study.

lead.text: With 6 people, one assignment in 20 puts the three highest outcomes in the treated arm by chance alone, and the p-value of 0.05 is the price of that possibility. Randomisation gives a *fair* comparison and tells you how often chance would make it look this good. It does not make the groups identical.

It also supports a claim only about the people who were randomised. If the people who agreed to join differ from the rest, the result may not carry over to them, which is the point of random sampling and a separate question from cause.

reveal.text: Counting the assignments shows in advance how small a p-value a design can ever deliver.

lessons.orientation: Explain why random assignment supports causal claims and count the assignments behind a randomisation p-value.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson looks at what happens when assignment is not random and a hidden factor drives both the treatment and the outcome.

blocks.text: When 200 people are offered a new drug and the 100 who take it recover more often than the 100 who do not, the difference has two possible sources. The drug may work, or the people who chose it may be the ones keen to get better, who rested, ate well and took their other medicine on time, and who would have done better with or without it. Nothing in the recovery data separates the two.

If a coin decides who gets the drug, no trait of the person can influence the choice, so the two arms are alike on average in everything except the treatment, and a difference between them can be attributed to the drug. This is what **random assignment** achieves and what careful matching on a few measured traits cannot, because a coin is indifferent to the traits that nobody thought to measure.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to explain why random assignment supports a causal claim and count the assignments behind a randomisation p-value.
intro.whyItMatters: Randomised experiments are the standard against which every other way of studying cause is judged.

recap.keyIdea: Random assignment balances every trait, measured or not, between the arms on average, and a randomisation p-value is a count of equally likely assignments.

blocks.text: A coin that decides each person's arm makes the arms alike on average in every trait, including the ones nobody measured, so a difference beyond chance can be attributed to the treatment. Blocking reduces noise and blinding reduces bias.
A randomisation test counts the equally likely assignments: 20 ways to pick 3 of 6 people, so the most extreme result has a one-sided p-value of 1/20.

lessons.title: When a hidden factor drives both

steps.headline: Pooled together, treatment B looks better than treatment A for kidney stones.

lead.text: A study of kidney stone treatments, published in the British Medical Journal in 1986 by Charig and colleagues, compared open surgery, which we will call treatment A, with a keyhole procedure, treatment B. Each was used on 350 patients, and the counts below are those widely reproduced from the paper. Treatment A succeeded in 273 of its 350 cases, which is 78 percent, and treatment B in 289 of 350, which is 83 percent.

On these totals B looks the better treatment by five percentage points, and a hospital reading the pooled figure would switch to it. Before doing so, it is worth asking how each patient came to be given each treatment, because nobody tossed a coin.

reveal.text: B does very well on small stones, 87 percent, and the next screen compares that with A on the same stones.

steps.headline: Within each stone size treatment A does better, and yet B wins overall, a reversal called Simpson's paradox.

lead.text: On small stones A succeeded in 81 of 87 cases, 93 percent, against B's 234 of 270, 87 percent. On large stones A succeeded in 192 of 263, 73 percent, against B's 55 of 80, 69 percent. A is better in *both* groups, and yet it is worse overall. Both statements are arithmetic, and the buttons in the figure let you check each.

A pooled comparison that reverses within every subgroup is called **Simpson's paradox**. It is a paradox only until you notice that the pooled rate is an average over the mix of cases, and that A and B were used on very different mixes.

steps.headline: The reversal happens because stone size drove which treatment was given and also how likely success was.

lead.text: Of A's 350 cases, 263 were large stones, whereas of B's 350 only 80 were, 23 percent. Doctors reserved the open surgery for the harder, larger stones, and large stones succeed less often whichever treatment is used. So A's pooled rate is dragged down by a harder mix of cases, and B's is lifted by an easier one, which is enough to hide that A is better within each group.

Stone size here influences *both* the treatment a patient received and the outcome. A variable that does this is a **confounder**, and the comparison that ignores it mixes the effect of the treatment with the effect of the stone size. The diagram shows its structure, with arrows from stone size to the other two.

afterFigure.text: Collecting more patients would not fix this. A thousand more cases with the same pattern of who gets which treatment would reproduce the reversal.

steps.headline: The remedy is to compare like with like within each stratum, and randomisation does it by design.

lead.text: The stone size table gives the fair comparison: within each size of stone, A is the better treatment. This is **stratifying**, comparing patients inside groups that are alike on the confounder and then, if a single figure is wanted, combining the groups with the *same* weights for both treatments. It works only for confounders that were recorded, and here stone size was.

Had the patients been randomised, a coin would have given each treatment about the same share of large stones and about the same of everything else, and the pooled figure would have been fair. That is the advantage of the last lesson: it balances the confounders nobody thought to record. Without it, one has to decide which variables matter and hope none is missing.

afterFigure.text: Be careful in turn about adjusting for everything. Some adjustments introduce bias, which the next lesson explains.

reveal.text: A beats B on large stones as well, so the claim that B is better rests only on the mix of cases.

blocks.text: In a study of kidney stone treatments published in 1986, treatment B succeeded in 83 percent of its cases and treatment A in 78 percent. Yet A had the higher success rate among small stones and also among large ones, so the overall comparison favoured B while every subgroup favoured A. The two results are consistent, because an overall rate is an average over whatever mixture of cases each treatment happened to receive.

Seeing why tells you when a pooled comparison answers a different question from the one you asked. The place to look is how each patient came to be given each treatment, since a reason for the choice that also affects the outcome makes the groups unlike before the treatment starts, and the remedy is to compare like with like.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to spot a confounder, show how pooling can reverse a comparison and fix it by comparing like with like.
intro.whyItMatters: Most claims of cause from observational data are made on pooled comparisons, and the pooled figure can point the wrong way.

recap.keyIdea: A confounder influences both the treatment and the outcome, so a pooled comparison can reverse what holds in every subgroup.

blocks.text: In the kidney stone data A wins on small and on large stones, yet B wins when they are pooled, because B was used mostly on the easier small stones. Stone size drives both the choice of treatment and the outcome.
Comparing like with like within strata corrects for a recorded confounder, and randomisation balances those nobody recorded. More data does not remove confounding.

lessons.title: Draw the causes

steps.headline: A fork is a common cause: one variable sends an arrow to two others, and the two then move together without either affecting the other.

lead.text: A causal diagram draws each variable once and puts an arrow from a cause to its effect. Take ice cream sales and drownings, which rise together across the days of a year. Draw an arrow from *heat* to each of them, and nothing between them. The pattern X ← Z → Y is called a **fork**, and the variable at its root, heat, is a common cause. This is the structure of a confounder from the last lesson.

The association between the two outcomes travels along the path that goes up one arrow and down the other. Compare only days with the *same* heat and that association has nothing to run on, so the path is **blocked**. This is what it means to adjust for a variable.

afterFigure.text: An arrow is a claim about what would change if we intervened, and the missing arrow between ice cream and drownings is a claim too: that changing one would not change the other.

steps.headline: In a chain the effect travels through a middle variable, and adjusting for that variable removes the very effect you may want.

lead.text: Smoking leaves tar in the lungs, and tar raises the chance of cancer, so the diagram is smoking → tar → cancer. The path is a **chain**, and its middle variable is a **mediator**. Smoking and cancer are associated, and in this diagram all of that association is the effect we care about.

Adjust for the mediator and the path is blocked, just as the fork was. Among people with equal tar in their lungs, smoking tells you nothing more about cancer, and a researcher who did this would wrongly conclude that smoking had no effect. The opposite rule from the fork follows: a variable on the causal path should usually be *left alone*.

steps.headline: In a collider two causes meet at one effect, and selecting on that effect makes the causes look related.

lead.text: The third shape reverses the arrows. Talent and looks each increase the chance of becoming a famous actor, so the diagram is talent → fame ← looks, and *fame* is a **collider**, a variable with two arrows pointing into it. In the whole population talent and looks may be unrelated, and the first view shows 300 people for whom their correlation is −0.04.

Now look only at the famous. Someone with little talent got there on looks and someone with plain looks got there on talent, so among the 32 famous people the correlation is −0.61. Selecting on the collider created a link that is not in the population. A collider path is therefore blocked until you adjust for it, and adjusting for it opens it.

afterFigure.text: Conditioning on a collider can arise without anyone choosing to, for example when a study includes only patients who reached hospital.

steps.headline: To find the effect of X on Y, block the backdoor paths created by common causes, leave the causal paths open and do not adjust for colliders.

lead.text: The three shapes give a rule. A **backdoor path** is a path from X to Y that begins with an arrow *into* X, as in X ← Z → Y. Each one carries a spurious association, so the variables that block them, usually the common causes, are adjusted for. A path that leaves X, such as X → M → Y, is a causal path and is left open, and a collider is left alone.

The figure shows a graph with two common causes, Z and W, and a mediator M. There are two backdoor paths, X ← Z → Y and X ← W → Y, and one causal path, X → M → Y. Adjusting for Z and W blocks both backdoor paths and leaves the effect measurable, whereas adjusting for M as well would block the causal path itself.

diagram.alt: A causal diagram with variables Z, W, M, X and Y. Z and W each point to X and to Y, so each creates a backdoor path. X points to M and M points to Y, which is the causal path. The three views show nothing adjusted, Z and W adjusted, and M adjusted as well.

steps.headline: A diagram is a set of claims from outside knowledge, and a missing arrow is the strongest claim in it.

lead.text: A causal diagram does not come out of the data. It is drawn from knowledge of how the variables work, and the same data are consistent with several diagrams. Every arrow says "changing this would change that", and every *missing* arrow says that it would not, which is a strong statement that the analysis then depends on. If you are unsure, draw the arrow in.

The rules above then do the work that guesswork would otherwise do. They say which variables to adjust for, which to leave alone and why adjusting for everything on hand is not safe: a mediator removes the effect, a collider adds bias, and only the common causes are worth adjusting for.

reveal.text: The right set is small. Adjusting for the collider would have introduced bias, which is the reason to read the arrows before adjusting.

blocks.text: Ice cream sales and drownings rise and fall together across the year, yet no one thinks that ice cream drowns people. Draw an arrow from heat to each of them and nothing between the two, and the drawing shows at a glance why they move together and why comparing only days of the same heat should make the link disappear. A drawing of this kind, with an arrow from each cause to its effects, is called a **causal diagram**.

Each way that arrows can connect three variables has a different effect on the association between the outer two. Knowing which is which gives a rule for choosing the variables to hold fixed when estimating an effect from data, and for spotting the ones to leave alone because holding them fixed would distort the answer.

blocks.text: A fork, a chain and a collider each connect two variables in a different way: a common cause makes them associated, a mediator carries the effect between them and a collider makes unrelated causes look related once it is selected on.
To find the effect of X on Y, adjust for the common causes that open backdoor paths, leave mediators alone and do not condition on colliders.
