lessons.title: When nature randomises

steps.headline: A rule or an accident can assign people to exposure in a way that has nothing to do with their outcome, and then the comparison is almost as good as a trial.

lead.text: In the London cholera epidemic of 1854, John Snow noticed that in some districts two water companies served houses on the very same streets. The Southwark and Vauxhall Company drew its water from the Thames below the sewage outfalls, and the Lambeth Company, which had moved its intake upstream in 1852, drew cleaner water. Which company supplied a house depended on the street's history and not on the household, so houses of rich and poor, old and new, were spread across both, much as a coin would spread them.

Snow counted cholera deaths by company and found far higher death rates in the houses served by Southwark and Vauxhall. Nobody had randomised, but the water companies had done something like it. Evidence of this kind, from a rule or accident that assigns exposure without regard to outcome, comes from a **natural experiment**.

reveal.text: The phrase "as if at random" is the claim that carries the whole design, and it has to be argued for from the facts, since no test can prove it.
Two points of the six would have happened anyway, and removing that shared trend is the idea of the next screen.

steps.headline: A difference in differences subtracts the control group's change from the treated group's change, so that trends the two groups share cancel out.

lead.text: Looking at the treated group alone, 50 to 56 is a rise of 6, but time moves outcomes by itself. The control group went from 48 to 50, a rise of 2 with no treatment. If the treated group would have risen by the same 2 without treatment, then only 6 − 2 = 4 is due to the treatment. This calculation, the treated change minus the control change, is the **difference in differences**.

The table in the figure fills in the steps in order. Note that the two groups do not need to start at the same level, 50 and 48 here. What is compared is how much each group *changed*, so any fixed difference between the groups drops out.

reveal.text: A control group lets you subtract the trend. Without it a before-and-after change in the treated group alone says very little.

steps.headline: The method works only if the groups would have changed alike without treatment, an assumption that cannot be tested directly.

lead.text: Subtracting the control change assumes that the treated group would have moved as the control group did if nothing had been done, which is the assumption of **parallel trends**. The dashed line in the figure is that unobserved path: the treated group at 52 instead of 56. The effect is the gap between where it ended up and where it would have been, which here is 4.

The assumption can be checked in part but not proved. Look at the earlier periods, before treatment. If the two groups moved in parallel then, as in the first view, the assumption is plausible. If the treated group was already rising faster, as in the second view, the estimate of 4 overstates the effect, which is only 2. Any comparison group will not do: it has to have followed the same trend.

afterFigure.text: A natural experiment is never better than the as-if randomness, or the parallel trends, that it relies on.

steps.headline: A cut-off gives a second kind of natural experiment, because people just either side of it are nearly alike.

lead.text: Suppose a scheme is open to everyone whose score is 18 or more. A person with 17.9 and one with 18.1 are almost the same, and which side of the line each falls on is close to luck. If the outcome climbs steadily with the score and then *jumps* at 18, as in the figure, the jump is the effect of the scheme. This design is called **regression discontinuity**.

It is credible only where people cannot manipulate their score to land just above the line, and it speaks only about people near the cut-off. All three designs of this lesson, the water companies, the difference in differences and the cut-off, trade the randomised trial for an assumption that has to be argued from what is known about how the exposure was assigned.

lessons.orientation: Compute a difference-in-differences and say what a natural experiment needs to be credible.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read an interval, a test and a regression, judge whether a study had enough data, and say whether a comparison supports a causal claim and what it would take to make it do so.

blocks.text: In 1854 John Snow found that houses on the same London streets were supplied with water by two different companies, one drawing from the Thames below the sewage outfalls and the other from cleaner water upstream. Nobody had decided who would drink which, so the households served by the two companies were much alike apart from their water, and a comparison of their cholera deaths came close to what a trial would have shown.

Where a trial is impossible, a rule or an accident of this kind sometimes does the assigning, and a comparison built on it can support a claim about cause. How far the claim can be believed depends on what is known about how the exposure came to be assigned, and on an assumption that has to be stated and argued because the data cannot prove it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a difference in differences and say what a natural experiment needs in order to be credible.
intro.whyItMatters: Many questions about cause cannot be settled by a trial, and a natural experiment is the best available substitute.

recap.keyIdea: A difference in differences subtracts the control group's change from the treated group's change, and it is credible only if the groups would have changed alike without treatment.

blocks.text: A natural experiment uses a rule or an accident that assigns exposure without regard to outcome. The difference in differences removes trends shared by both groups, and a cut-off gives a jump in the outcome between nearly alike people.
Each design rests on an assumption about how exposure was assigned, parallel trends or no manipulation of the cut-off, which cannot be proved and has to be argued from what is known.

questions.prompt: Two values are drawn at random from 2, 4 and 6, with the first put back before the second, and their mean is taken. Which mean comes up most often across the nine equally likely samples?
hints: Write the nine ordered pairs out and average each.
Count how many pairs give each mean. Order matters, so (2, 6) and (6, 2) are different samples.

acceptedIdeas: A mean of 4, the population mean
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mean of 4, the population mean

questions.onCorrect: A mean of 4 is made by (2, 6), (4, 4) and (6, 2), more ways than any other, which is why the nine means pile up around the population mean.

misconceptions.feedback: The nine samples are equally likely, but they do not give nine different means. Several samples share a mean, and some means can be made in more ways than others.
A mean of 2 needs both draws to be 2, which is one sample out of the nine. A mean of 4 can be made in three ways.

choices.label: A mean of 4, the population mean
A mean of 2, the smallest value
All the means are equally likely

questions.prompt: Averaging two draws from 2, 4 and 6 gave sample means with variance 4/3, half the population variance of 8/3. Suppose three values were drawn each time, each put back before the next. What would you expect the variance of the sample means to be?
hints: Averaging two draws halved the variance. Ask what happens when a third draw joins the average.
Compare the divisor for two draws with the number of draws.

acceptedIdeas: About 8/9, a third of the population variance, since more draws cancel more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 8/9, a third of the population variance, since more draws cancel more

questions.onCorrect: The variance of the sample mean is the population variance divided by the number of draws, so three draws give 8/3 divided by 3, which is 8/9.

misconceptions.feedback: Each draw does come from the same values, but a mean of three draws lets highs and lows cancel, so the means vary less than single values do. Two draws already halved the variance.
A third draw cancels still more of the variation, so the variance keeps falling as the sample grows. Two draws gave half the population variance.

choices.label: About 8/3, the same as the population, since every draw comes from the same three values
About 4/3, the same as for two draws, since the variance has already been halved
About 8/9, a third of the population variance, since more draws cancel more

questions.prompt: Why is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n and not by n?
hints: Start from the variance of the mean, which is the variance divided by n.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

acceptedIdeas: Averaging n values divides the variance by n, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Averaging n values divides the variance by n, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

questions.onCorrect: The variance of a mean is the variance divided by n, and the standard error is the square root of that.

misconceptions.feedback: The root has nothing to do with whole numbers. It undoes the squaring in the variance.
Dividing by n would shrink the spread far too fast. The variance is divided by n, so the sd is divided by the square root.

choices.label: Averaging n values divides the variance by n, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
The sample standard deviation is always the population one divided by n.
The square root only serves to turn the answer into a whole number.

questions.prompt: With sd 12 and n = 144, what is the standard error?
hints: Find the square root of 144 first.
Divide the sd by that root.
The root of 144 is 12.
questions.onCorrect: Quadrupling n from 36 to 144 took the square root from 6 to 12 and halved the standard error from 2 to 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 144 itself. The divisor is the square root of n.
That is the standard error for n = 36.

questions.prompt: A measurement has sd 20. How large must n be for the standard error to fall to 2?
hints: Set 20 divided by the square root of n equal to 2.
Solve for the square root of n first.
Then square it to get n.
questions.onCorrect: To reach a target standard error, square the ratio sd / SE: (20 / 2) squared is 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the square root of n. Square it to get n.
The error does not fall in proportion to n. Solve 20 / sqrt(n) = 2 properly.

questions.prompt: A poll in a town of 50,000 people has sd 10 and n = 100, so its standard error is 1. The same poll in a city of 5,000,000 people also has sd 10 and n = 100. How does its standard error compare?
hints: Write the formula for the standard error and look for the population size in it.
Both polls have the same sd and the same n.

acceptedIdeas: About 1, the same as in the town, because only the sd and n enter the formula
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1, the same as in the town, because only the sd and n enter the formula

questions.onCorrect: The population size matters only when the sample is a large fraction of it, which is far from true in both of these polls.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula contains the sd and n and nothing about the size of the population. Both polls divide an sd of 10 by the square root of 100.
A bigger population can have a different sd, but here the sd is the same 10 in both, and the standard error follows from the sd and n alone.

choices.label: Larger than 1, because a bigger population has more variety in it
Smaller than 1, because 100 people are a tinier share of the city
About 1, the same as in the town, because only the sd and n enter the formula

questions.prompt: A population has sd 15. What is the standard error of the mean for samples of size 25?
hints: Use SE = sd / sqrt(n).
The square root of 25 is 5.
Divide the sd by that root.
questions.onCorrect: The standard error is the sd of the sample mean, here a fifth of the sd of single values.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by n = 25 rather than its square root.
That is the sd of the data, not of the mean.
The sd is divided by the root of n, not multiplied.

questions.prompt: The sd is 14. How large must n be for the standard error to be 2?
hints: Set 14 / sqrt(n) equal to 2.
Solve for the square root of n first.
Square that result to get n.
questions.onCorrect: The sample size needed is (sd / SE) squared, here (14 / 2) squared.

misconceptions.feedback: That is sqrt(n). Square it to get n.
That multiplies 14 by 2. Divide first, then square.

questions.prompt: A pilot sample gives a certain standard error. How much larger must the sample be to halve it?
hints: The standard error contains the square root of n.
To halve 1 / sqrt(n), the root of n must double.

acceptedIdeas: Four times as large
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Four times as large

questions.onCorrect: Halving the standard error needs a sample four times as large, because the error falls with the square root of n.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling n divides the error by only about 1.41, the square root of 2.
Eight times as large would cut the error by about 2.83, more than needed.
Care does not change the formula. The error depends on n and the spread of the data.

choices.label: Eight times as large
Four times as large
The same size, but sampled more carefully
Twice as large

questions.prompt: Scores have mean 500 and sd 100. What is the z-score of 650?
hints: Subtract the mean from the value.
Divide that difference by the standard deviation.
questions.onCorrect: The score sits one and a half standard deviations above the mean, whatever the units were.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance in score points. Divide by the sd to get standard deviations.
The value is above the mean, so the z-score is positive.

questions.prompt: What is the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean called?
hints: It is named after the letter used in the formula.
The letter in z = (x − mean) / sd.

acceptedIdeas: z-score
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: z-score

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls

questions.onCorrect: A stricter threshold rejects less often, including when the effect is real, so power falls unless the sample grows.

misconceptions.feedback: A stricter threshold makes rejection rarer, which cannot raise the share of real effects that are caught.
The cut-off moves, and the area of the effect curve that falls on the wrong side grows.
A power of 1 would mean every real effect is caught, which a stricter threshold makes less likely.

choices.label: It stays the same
It rises
It becomes 1
It falls

questions.prompt: A real effect of 3, an sd of 10 and n = 100. How many standard errors from zero does the real effect sit?
hints: Find the standard error of the mean first.
SE = sd / sqrt(n) = 10 / 10.
Divide the effect by the standard error.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: SE = 10 / 10 = 1, so the effect sits 3 / 1 = 3 standard errors from zero.

questions.onCorrect: The distance from zero in standard errors is what the power depends on, along with the cut-off.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the effect by the sd. The distance that matters is counted in standard errors.
The effect divided by SE, not multiplied.

questions.prompt: With n = 25, a real effect of 5 and an sd of 10, the effect sits 2.5 standard errors from zero. If n is raised to 100, how far from zero will the same effect sit?
hints: Recall what quadrupling n does to the standard error.
Halving the standard error doubles any distance counted in standard errors.

acceptedIdeas: 5 standard errors, twice as far
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 5 standard errors, twice as far

questions.onCorrect: The distance grows with the square root of n, so four times the data doubled it from 2.5 to 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That would need 16 times the data. The standard error falls with the square root of n, so quadrupling n only doubles the distance.
The effect has not changed, but the standard error has. It falls from 2 to 1 when n goes from 25 to 100, so the effect sits further out in standard errors.

choices.label: 2.5 standard errors, the same as before, because the effect has not changed
5 standard errors, twice as far
10 standard errors, four times as far

questions.prompt: In the worked power calculation, why does the second term, Φ(−2 − 1.96), add almost nothing?
hints: The real effect curve is centred above zero.
How much of that curve lies beyond −1.96?

acceptedIdeas: It is the chance of landing far below zero when the real effect is above it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the chance of landing far below zero when the real effect is above it.

questions.onCorrect: The lower rejection region is so far from the real-effect curve that it contributes about 0.00004 to the power.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 is larger than 1.96, which is why the power is just over 0.5.
Both terms are added. The second is just very small.

choices.label: Because 2 is smaller than 1.96.
It is the chance of landing far below zero when the real effect is above it.
Because the second term is subtracted.

questions.prompt: Work out the smallest whole sample size. The calculation gives (2.8016 × 3)² = 70.6.
hints: A sample size must be a whole number.
Would 70 people reach 80 percent power?
Always round up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sample size must be a whole number, and rounding down would leave the power below 80 percent, so round up to 71.

questions.onCorrect: Round the sample size up, since 70 people would fall slightly short of 80 percent power.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds down, which leaves the power slightly under 80 percent.
The sample has to be a whole number of people.

questions.prompt: Effect 5 and sd 10 needed 32 people for 80 percent power. Now the smallest effect that matters is 2.5. What is the smallest whole n? Use 1.96 and 0.8416.
hints: Halving the effect doubles the ratio sd / effect.
Doubling that ratio multiplies n by 4.
Or compute (2.8016 × 10 / 2.5)² and round up.
questions.onCorrect: Halving the effect to be detected needs four times the sample, which is why chasing small effects is expensive.

misconceptions.feedback: Round up, not down, so that the power stays at or above 80 percent.
Halving the effect does not halve n. n goes with the inverse square of the effect.

questions.prompt: Effect 3, sd 10, n = 100, alpha 0.05 two-sided. Using the normal model, what is the power to two decimals?
hints: Find the standard error and the distance in standard errors.
The distance is 3. Subtract 1.96.
Use the area below z = 1.04 from a table.
questions.onCorrect: About 85 percent of such studies would reject, so about 15 percent would miss an effect of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the missed-effect rate. Power is its complement.
That would be the power if the effect sat exactly on the cut-off.

questions.prompt: Effect 3, sd 10, alpha 0.05, 80 percent power. Use 1.96 and 0.8416. What is the smallest whole n?
hints: Add 1.96 and 0.8416, multiply by sd / effect.
The product is about 9.34.
Square it and round up.
questions.onCorrect: The planned sample is 88, rounded up from 87.2.

misconceptions.feedback: Rounding down leaves the power slightly under 80 percent.
That is the quantity before squaring.

questions.prompt: Which change raises power?
hints: Power depends on the effect, the spread, n and alpha.
Which of these changes moves the real-effect curve further from zero in standard errors?

acceptedIdeas: A larger sample
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A larger sample

questions.onCorrect: A larger sample shrinks the standard error, which moves the real effect further from zero in standard-error units.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller sample enlarges the standard error and so lowers power.
A smaller effect lies closer to zero and is harder to catch.
A noisier measure raises the sd and so the standard error, which lowers power.

choices.label: A smaller sample
A smaller effect
A noisier measure
A larger sample

questions.prompt: Two groups each have sd 10 and n = 25. What is the standard error of the difference in their means, to two decimals?
hints: Find the variance of each group mean, sd squared over n.
Each is 100 / 25 = 4.
Add the variances, then take the square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each variance of a mean is 100 / 25 = 4, and sqrt(4 + 4) = sqrt(8) = 2.83.

questions.onCorrect: Variances add, so the SE of a difference is larger than either group alone, but smaller than the sum of the two standard errors, 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the standard errors, 2 and 2. Variances add, and the square root is taken after.
That is the standard error of one group alone.

questions.prompt: Why is the standard error of a difference the square root of the sum of squares and not the sum?
hints: Which quantity adds for independent estimates: standard deviations or variances?
The standard error is a standard deviation.

acceptedIdeas: Variances of independent estimates add, and the standard error is the square root of a variance.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variances of independent estimates add, and the standard error is the square root of a variance.

questions.onCorrect: For independent estimates the variances add, so the standard error is the square root of the sum of the squared standard errors.

misconceptions.feedback: Squares appear because variances, not standard errors, add. The subtraction does not matter, since each estimate adds its own noise.
Adding the standard errors gives a larger value, so the interval would be too wide, not too narrow.

choices.label: Adding the standard errors would give an interval that is too narrow.
Squares are always used when two numbers are subtracted.
Variances of independent estimates add, and the standard error is the square root of a variance.

questions.prompt: Groups C and D give a difference of 5 and a standard error of 2. What is the margin of error for a 95 percent interval? Use 1.96.
hints: The margin is the critical value times the standard error.
questions.onCorrect: The interval is 5 ± 3.92, or (1.08, 8.92), which excludes zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the standard error. Multiply it by 1.96.
That multiplies by 1.96 twice over; one multiplication is enough.

questions.prompt: Four people are measured before and after a treatment. Before: 10, 12, 9, 14. After: 8, 11, 9, 11. Taking each person's change as after minus before, what is the mean change?
hints: Work out after − before for each person.
Add the four changes and divide by 4.

acceptedIdeas: A fall of 1.5, because the changes are −2, −1, 0 and −3
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fall of 1.5, because the changes are −2, −1, 0 and −3

questions.onCorrect: Taking the difference person by person turns two columns of data into one column of changes.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign matters. After is lower than before for three of the four people and equal for the fourth, so each change is zero or negative.
The changes are worked out person by person. Three of the four people fell and none rose, so the average change cannot be zero.

choices.label: A rise of 1.5, because the changes add up to 6
No change, because the after values fall within the range of the before values
A fall of 1.5, because the changes are −2, −1, 0 and −3

questions.prompt: Nine changes have mean −2.4 and sd 1.8, so SE = 1.8 / 3 = 0.6. With 8 degrees of freedom t = 2.306. What is the margin of error, to two decimals?
hints: Multiply the t value by the standard error.
The product is a little under 1.4.
questions.onCorrect: The interval is −2.4 ± 1.38, or (−3.78, −1.02), which excludes zero, so changes this consistent across nine people do show a fall.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the standard error. Multiply it by 2.306.
That uses 1.96. With 8 degrees of freedom the t value is 2.306.

questions.prompt: Twenty-five patients each have a before and after reading. The changes have mean −6 and sd 10, so SE = 2. With t(24) = 2.064, what is the upper end of the 95 percent interval for the mean change?
hints: The margin is the t value times the standard error.
Add the margin to the mean change of −6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The margin is 2.064 × 2 = 4.128, so the upper end is −6 + 4.128 = −1.872, about −1.87.

questions.onCorrect: The whole interval, −10.13 to −1.87, lies below zero, so the readings did fall.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the lower end. The question asks for the upper end.
That is the margin of error. Add it to the mean of −6.

questions.prompt: Group 1 has sd 6 and n = 36. Group 2 has sd 8 and n = 64. What is the standard error of the difference in means, to two decimals?
hints: Find sd squared divided by n for each group.
Each comes to 1.
Add them and take the square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The variances of the means are 36/36 = 1 and 64/64 = 1, and sqrt(1 + 1) = 1.41.

questions.onCorrect: The standard error of a difference combines the variances of the two means, then takes the square root.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the standard errors. Add the variances, 1 and 1, and then take the square root.
That is the standard error for one group. Combine both.

questions.prompt: Before: 20, 25, 30, 35. After: 18, 22, 31, 30. What is the mean of (after − before)?
hints: Subtract each before value from the matching after value.
The changes are −2, −3, 1 and −5.
Add them and divide by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The changes are −2, −3, 1 and −5, which sum to −9, and −9 / 4 = −2.25.

questions.onCorrect: Pairing works with the changes, so the mean change, −2.25, is what the analysis is about.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign matters. The values went down on average, so the mean change is negative.
That is the mean of the before values. Subtract before from after for each person.

questions.prompt: Which study should use a paired analysis?
hints: Pairing needs each value in one group to be matched with a value in the other.
Which study measures the same people twice?

acceptedIdeas: Blood pressure of the same patients before and after a drug
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Blood pressure of the same patients before and after a drug

questions.onCorrect: Measuring the same patients twice gives matched pairs, and the analysis works with the change for each patient.

misconceptions.feedback: The patients on A and B are different people, so there are no pairs.
Two unrelated classes have no matching between their members.
Random samples of students are independent groups with no match.

choices.label: Blood pressure of patients on drug A against different patients on drug B
Heights of two unrelated classes
Scores of two random samples of students
Blood pressure of the same patients before and after a drug

questions.prompt: Six independent tests are run on true nulls, each at alpha 0.05. What is the probability of at least one false rejection, to two decimals?
hints: First find the chance that none of the six rejects.
That chance is 0.95 multiplied by itself 6 times.
Subtract it from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Even six tests raise the chance of at least one false alarm from 5 percent to more than a quarter.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the six alphas. The tests overlap, so the true figure is a little lower.
That is the chance of no false alarm. The question asks for at least one.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the correction that divides alpha by the number of tests?
hints: It is named after an Italian mathematician.
It begins with a B.

acceptedIdeas: Bonferroni correction
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bonferroni correction

questions.onCorrect: The Bonferroni correction keeps the chance of any false alarm at or below the original alpha.

misconceptions.feedback: Holm is a refinement of this correction. The plain one, which divides alpha by the number of tests, is older.

questions.prompt: Five comparisons are made, and the overall chance of any false alarm is to stay at 0.05. What threshold should each comparison use?
hints: The threshold for each test has to be stricter than the overall one.
Share 0.05 among the five tests.

acceptedIdeas: 0.01, which is 0.05 shared among the five
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0.01, which is 0.05 shared among the five

questions.onCorrect: Each test must pass a stricter bar, 0.01, so that the five together stay near 0.05.

misconceptions.feedback: At 0.05 each, five tests on true nulls would give at least one false alarm about 23 percent of the time. The threshold has to be shared out among the tests.
A larger threshold passes more results, so it gives more false alarms. The threshold is divided by the number of tests, not multiplied.

choices.label: 0.05, since each comparison is a test in its own right
0.25, which is 0.05 multiplied by five
0.01, which is 0.05 shared among the five

questions.prompt: Why is the chance of at least one false alarm in 25 tests 1 − 0.95^25, and not 25 × 0.05?
hints: What is the chance that none of the 25 tests rejects?
Could a chance above 1 be right for 25 tests at 0.05?

acceptedIdeas: It is easier to find the chance of no false alarm and subtract from 1, and 25 × 0.05 would exceed 1, which cannot be right.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is easier to find the chance of no false alarm and subtract from 1, and 25 × 0.05 would exceed 1, which cannot be right.

questions.onCorrect: The chance of no false alarm is 0.95^25 = 0.277, so at least one has chance 0.723. Adding the alphas counts overlaps twice.

misconceptions.feedback: 0.95 is the chance a single test does not reject a true null, which is 1 − alpha.
Independence is what lets the 0.95 values be multiplied.

choices.label: Because 0.95 is the power of each test.
Because the tests are not independent.
It is easier to find the chance of no false alarm and subtract from 1, and 25 × 0.05 would exceed 1, which cannot be right.

questions.prompt: Twelve independent tests of true nulls at alpha 0.05. What is the probability of at least one false rejection, to two decimals?
hints: Find 0.95 multiplied by itself 12 times.
Subtract from 1.
questions.onCorrect: With twelve tests the odds of at least one false alarm are close to even.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of no false alarm. Subtract it from 1.
That is 12 × 0.05. The tests overlap, so the exact figure is lower.

questions.prompt: A researcher slices the data 30 ways and finds one slice with p = 0.02. Is that slice significant at an overall level of 0.05 once the Bonferroni correction is applied?
hints: Divide the overall alpha by the number of tests.
Compare the p-value with the corrected threshold.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the corrected threshold is 0.05 / 30, about 0.0017, and 0.02 is above it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the corrected threshold is 0.05 / 30, about 0.0017, and 0.02 is above it

questions.onCorrect: A p of 0.02 is well above 0.0017, so the best of 30 slices does not stand out from what chance alone produces.

misconceptions.feedback: 0.05 is the threshold for a single test. With 30 tests the corrected threshold is 0.05 / 30, about 0.0017, and 0.02 does not reach it.
The Bonferroni correction keeps the family-wise error rate at or below 0.05 however the tests are related, so it applies to the 30 slices as they stand.

choices.label: No, because the corrected threshold is 0.05 / 30, about 0.0017, and 0.02 is above it
Not decided, because the correction only works when the 30 slices are independent
Yes, because 0.02 is below 0.05

questions.prompt: 15 independent tests of true nulls at alpha 0.05. What is the probability of at least one false rejection, to two decimals?
hints: Find the chance that none of the fifteen tests rejects.
That is 0.95 multiplied by itself 15 times.
Subtract from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Fifteen tests at 0.05 each give a better than even chance of at least one false alarm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of no false alarm, 0.95^15. Subtract from 1.
That is 15 × 0.05. The tests overlap, so the true figure is lower.

questions.prompt: Eight comparisons with an overall alpha of 0.05. What is the Bonferroni per-test threshold?
hints: Divide the overall alpha by the number of comparisons.
0.05 divided by 8.
The result is smaller than the overall alpha.
questions.onCorrect: Each of the eight tests has to reach p below 0.00625 to count as a finding.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of at least one false alarm across 8 tests with no correction. The threshold is alpha divided by 8.

questions.prompt: A researcher tries 30 subgroups and reports the one with p = 0.02. What is the main problem?
hints: How many chances did the researcher have to find a small p-value?
What would the chance of at least one p below 0.05 be among 30 true nulls?

acceptedIdeas: The reported p-value ignores the 30 comparisons
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reported p-value ignores the 30 comparisons

questions.onCorrect: The reported p-value was the best of 30, so it overstates the evidence, and a correction for 30 tests would be needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Subgroups can be valid when they are planned and counted. The fault is hiding how many were tried.
Small p-values can be real. This one ignores that it was picked out from 30.
A large sample is not a fault. It is the selection among 30 results that misleads.

choices.label: The sample was too large
The reported p-value ignores the 30 comparisons
Subgroups are never valid
p = 0.02 is too small to be real

questions.prompt: A least-squares line has slope 1.5, and its data have a mean x of 4 and a mean y of 9, so the line passes through (4, 9). What is its intercept, the value of y when x = 0?
hints: The line passes through the point of means.
Work out the slope times the mean of x.
Subtract that from the mean of y.
questions.onCorrect: Every least-squares line passes through the point (x̄, ȳ), which fixes its intercept once the slope is known.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the slope times x̄. Subtract it from ȳ = 9.
That is the mean of y, which is the height of the line at x̄ and not at x = 0.

questions.prompt: The line is y = 0.7 + 2.2x. What does it predict at x = 3?
hints: Put 3 in place of x.
Add the intercept 0.7.
questions.onCorrect: The prediction is 7.3, a little below the observed 8, so the point sits above the line.

misconceptions.feedback: That omits the intercept of 0.7.
That is the observed value at x = 3, not the prediction.

questions.prompt: A line y = 1 + 2x is fitted to some data. At x = 3 the observed y is 6.2. What is the residual, observed minus predicted?
hints: First find the line's prediction at x = 3.
Subtract the prediction from the observed 6.2. The point lies below the line, so the sign is negative.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line predicts 1 + 2 × 3 = 7, so the residual is 6.2 − 7 = −0.8.

questions.onCorrect: A negative residual means the point lies below the line. The residuals of a least-squares line add to zero.

misconceptions.feedback: The residual is observed minus predicted, so a point below the line has a negative residual.
That is the prediction. Subtract it from the observed 6.2.

questions.prompt: Which point does every least-squares line pass through?
hints: Think about where the line balances the data.
The intercept formula uses both means.

acceptedIdeas: The point (mean of x, mean of y)
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The point (mean of x, mean of y)

questions.onCorrect: A least-squares line always passes through (x̄, ȳ), which is why the intercept equals ȳ minus the slope times x̄.

misconceptions.feedback: Only a line fitted through the origin would do that, and a least-squares line has a free intercept.
The line balances all the points together, so it need not touch any of them.

choices.label: The point (mean of x, mean of y)
The origin, (0, 0)
The first data point

questions.prompt: The points (1, 3), (2, 5) and (3, 10) have x̄ = 2 and ȳ = 6, with Sxy = 7 and Sxx = 2. What is the slope?
hints: The slope is Sxy divided by Sxx.
Both sums are given.
7 divided by 2.
questions.onCorrect: The slope is the sum of products of the deviations over the sum of squared deviations in x, here 7 / 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Sxy. Divide it by Sxx = 2.
That is Sxx. The slope is Sxy / Sxx.

questions.prompt: The line weight = 3.8 + 0.5 × age, with weight in kilograms and age in months, was fitted to infants aged 1 to 12 months. At 30 years, an age of 360 months, it gives a weight of 183.8 kg. What does that result show?
hints: Compare 183.8 kg with the weight of a typical adult.
Ask which ages the line was fitted on and which age it is being used for.

acceptedIdeas: The line should not be trusted at ages far outside the 1 to 12 months it was fitted on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The line should not be trusted at ages far outside the 1 to 12 months it was fitted on

questions.onCorrect: The arithmetic is right, but 183.8 kg is far beyond a typical adult. The line only describes the ages it was fitted on.

misconceptions.feedback: A good fit within the first year says nothing about ages far beyond it. Here the line gives a weight that few adults reach.
The slope is a fair summary of growth in the first year. What fails is applying the line at an age far from any of the data.

choices.label: The line should not be trusted at ages far outside the 1 to 12 months it was fitted on
The line is a good summary of weight at every age, since it fits the infants well
The slope of 0.5 kg a month must be wrong, since no one gains that much for 30 years

questions.prompt: Points (1, 2), (2, 3) and (3, 7). The mean of x is 2 and the mean of y is 4. What is the least-squares slope?
hints: Find each deviation from the means, then multiply the pairs and add.
Sxy is 5. Find Sxx, the sum of squared deviations in x.
Divide Sxy by Sxx.
questions.onCorrect: The slope is Sxy / Sxx, which weights each point by how far its x lies from the mean.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Sxy. Divide it by Sxx = 2.
That is Sxx. The slope is Sxy over Sxx.
That is the mean of y, not a slope.

questions.prompt: A line is y = 0.7 + 2.2x. At x = 5 what does it predict?
hints: Put 5 in place of x.
Add the intercept.
questions.onCorrect: A prediction is the intercept plus the slope times x, here at a value one step past the points that were used.

misconceptions.feedback: That omits the intercept of 0.7.
That is the prediction at x = 1.

questions.prompt: Across a primary school, children with larger shoe sizes have higher reading scores, and the fitted slope is positive. What is the safest reading?
hints: A fitted slope describes how two variables move together.
What else could raise both?

acceptedIdeas: The two move together, but the data alone do not show that either causes the other
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two move together, but the data alone do not show that either causes the other

questions.onCorrect: A slope describes association. Older children have both larger feet and better reading, and the data alone cannot separate that from a causal link.

misconceptions.feedback: The slope shows that the two rise together, not that one makes the other happen.
The data show no direction of cause. Neither reading follows from the slope.
The slope can be correct and still not show cause. The problem is the interpretation.

choices.label: Larger feet improve reading
The two move together, but the data alone do not show that either causes the other
The slope must be wrong
Reading makes feet grow

questions.prompt: A coin decides which arm each of 200 people joins, and 100 of them are keen to get better. About how many of the keen people would you expect to find in the drug arm?
hints: The coin does not know who is keen.
Each keen person has the same chance of either arm.

acceptedIdeas: About 50, because the coin treats keen and other people alike
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 50, because the coin treats keen and other people alike

questions.onCorrect: A fair coin sends about half of any trait, measured or not, to each arm, though in one small trial the split is rarely exactly even.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number when the keen people choose for themselves. A coin ignores keenness, so keen people are no more likely to land in the drug arm.
A fair coin sends about half of any trait to each arm on average, but in one small trial the split is rarely exactly even.

choices.label: About 80, as when the keen people chose for themselves
Exactly 50 in every trial, because a coin guarantees equal groups
About 50, because the coin treats keen and other people alike

questions.prompt: In a trial of a new drug, the control group is the arm that does not receive the drug. What is the control group for?
hints: A difference in recovery only means something next to another group.
Ask what the treated arm would be compared with if there were no second arm.

acceptedIdeas: It shows how people recover without the drug, so the treated arm has something to be compared with
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It shows how people recover without the drug, so the treated arm has something to be compared with

questions.onCorrect: Without a control group there is nothing to compare the treated group against, and a coin makes the two groups alike apart from the drug.

misconceptions.feedback: That is blinding. The control group has a different job, which is to supply the comparison.
Both arms are formed by the coin at the start. The control group is not a reserve for the treated arm.

choices.label: It shows how people recover without the drug, so the treated arm has something to be compared with
It takes the place of the treated arm if too few people agree to take the drug
It hides from the participants which arm they are in, so that expectation cannot shape the outcome

questions.prompt: Counting the ways to pick 3 treated people out of 7 divides 7 × 6 × 5 by 3 × 2 × 1. Why?
hints: If you pick A, then B, then C, or C, then B, then A, do you get a different group?
How many orders are there for 3 people?

acceptedIdeas: The order in which the treated people are picked does not matter, so each group is counted 3 × 2 × 1 times.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The order in which the treated people are picked does not matter, so each group is counted 3 × 2 × 1 times.

questions.onCorrect: There are 7 × 6 × 5 = 210 ordered picks and each unordered group of 3 appears 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 times, so 210 / 6 = 35 groups.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the control group has 4 people, more than the 3 treated, and the division has nothing to do with its size.
The division does give a whole number, but it is made because the picking order is irrelevant.

choices.label: The order in which the treated people are picked does not matter, so each group is counted 3 × 2 × 1 times.
Because 35 must come out as a whole number.
Because the control group is always smaller.

questions.prompt: 10 people are split into two labelled groups of 5. How many different assignments are possible?
hints: Count the ways to choose which 5 go in the first group.
The numerator is 30,240.
questions.onCorrect: There are 252 equally likely assignments, so the smallest possible one-sided randomisation p-value with 10 people is 1/252.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half of 20 or the number of people, and neither counts the ways of choosing.
That is the number of ordered picks. Divide by 5! to remove the order.

questions.prompt: Five people are split into a treated group of 2 and a control group of 3. If the 2 treated people have the 2 highest outcomes, what is the one-sided randomisation p-value?
hints: Count the possible assignments first.
Choosing 2 of 5 gives 5 × 4 / 2.
One assignment is as extreme as the actual one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 10 ways to choose 2 treated people from 5, and one of them is this extreme, so p = 1/10 = 0.1.

questions.onCorrect: With so few people no result can have a p-value below 0.1, so a trial this small cannot show a significant effect however large it is.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the p-value with 20 assignments. With 5 people there are only 10.
That would be 2 of 10, which would count a second assignment as extreme.

questions.prompt: 8 people are split into two labelled groups of 4. How many different assignments are possible?
hints: Count the ways to choose which 4 go in the first group.
The numerator is 1,680.
questions.onCorrect: There are 70 equally likely assignments, so the smallest possible one-sided p-value is 1/70.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of ordered picks. Divide by 4! = 24.
That is the count when the two groups are not labelled, so each split is counted once rather than twice.

questions.prompt: What does random assignment accomplish that matching on age and sex does not?
hints: Matching can only balance the traits that were measured.
A coin ignores every trait, measured or not.

acceptedIdeas: It balances unmeasured traits on average
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It balances unmeasured traits on average

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment balances every trait on average, including those nobody measured, and the p-value accounts for the chance imbalance that remains.

misconceptions.feedback: Randomising does not guarantee equal groups. A small trial can by chance end up unbalanced, which the p-value allows for.
A control group is still needed. Randomising only decides who goes in which arm.
Representativeness comes from how people were sampled, which is a different matter from how they are assigned.

choices.label: It guarantees identical groups
It removes the need for a control group
It balances unmeasured traits on average
It makes the sample representative

questions.prompt: What is the name for hiding the arm from participants so that expectation does not shape the outcome?
hints: The participant cannot see which arm they are in.
It is also called masking.

acceptedIdeas: blinding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: blinding

questions.onCorrect: In a double-blind trial neither the participants nor those measuring the outcome know the arms.

misconceptions.feedback: A placebo is the dummy treatment, not the act of hiding which arm someone is in.

questions.prompt: What is the name for sorting people into groups of similar people first and then randomising within each group?
hints: The groups are formed before the coin is used.
It reduces noise and does not by itself remove bias.

acceptedIdeas: blocking
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: blocking

questions.onCorrect: Blocking guarantees the arms are alike on the blocking trait and makes the comparison less noisy.

misconceptions.feedback: Stratified sampling concerns how people are drawn from a population. Sorting people before assigning them has a different name.

questions.prompt: Treatment B succeeded in 234 of 270 small-stone cases. What is its success rate as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number?
hints: Divide the successes by the number of cases.
234 divided by 270.
Multiply the result by 100.
questions.onCorrect: B does well on small stones, and most of its cases were small ones, which is what lifts its pooled rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B's pooled rate over all stones. This question is about small stones only.
The answer is asked as a percentage, so multiply by 100.

questions.prompt: Treatment A was used on 350 cases, of which 263 were large stones. What percentage of its cases were large stones, rounded to the nearest whole number?
hints: Divide the large-stone cases by all the cases A treated.
263 divided by 350.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Three in four of A's cases were the harder, large stones, against fewer than one in four of B's.

misconceptions.feedback: That is A's success rate on large stones. The question asks what share of its cases were large.
That is the share of B's cases that were large stones.

questions.prompt: Why does B's pooled rate come out higher than A's although A wins in each group?
hints: Look at how many of each treatment's cases were small and how many were large.
Which stones succeed more often?

acceptedIdeas: Most of B's cases were small stones, which are easier to treat.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of B's cases were small stones, which are easier to treat.

questions.onCorrect: B was used mostly on small stones, which succeed more often, so its pooled rate benefits from an easier mix of cases.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the data suggests that. The difference in the mix of cases accounts for the reversal.
Neither the pooled nor the stratified figures are right automatically. The right comparison depends on how cases came to be in each arm.

choices.label: B was applied more carefully.
Most of B's cases were small stones, which are easier to treat.
The pooled rate is always the correct one.

questions.prompt: What name is given to a variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome, and so distorts their comparison?
hints: It is the hidden factor in the diagram, stone size.
Its name comes from a word meaning to mix up.

acceptedIdeas: confounder
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: confounder

questions.onCorrect: A confounder affects both who gets the treatment and how the outcome turns out, so it must be dealt with before the comparison can be read as an effect.

misconceptions.feedback: A mediator lies on the path from treatment to outcome. The variable asked about sits behind both.

questions.prompt: Treatment A succeeded in 81 of 87 small-stone cases and 192 of 263 large-stone cases. What is its overall success rate as a percentage, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Add the successes from both groups and the cases from both groups.
273 successes in 350 cases.
Divide and multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The pooled rate weights each group by how many cases it contains, which is why the mix of cases matters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B's pooled rate. Add A's own successes and cases.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical treatment C succeeded in 54 of 60 small-stone cases and 70 of 140 large-stone cases. What is its overall success rate as a percentage, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Add the successes and the cases across both groups.
124 successes in 200 cases.
Divide and multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: C's pooled rate sits much nearer its large-stone rate of 50 percent than its small-stone rate of 90 percent, because 70 percent of its cases were large stones.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the two rates, 90 and 50 percent, as if each size had the same number of cases. Add the successes and the cases instead.

questions.prompt: Treatment B succeeded in 55 of 80 large-stone cases. What is its success rate as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number?
hints: Divide the successes by the cases.
55 divided by 80.
Multiply by 100 and round.
questions.onCorrect: Against A's 73 percent on large stones, B is lower, so A wins on large stones as well as on small ones.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B's pooled rate. This question is about large stones only.
That is A's rate on large stones.

questions.prompt: Treatment A succeeded in 192 of 263 large-stone cases. What is the success rate as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number?
hints: Divide the successes by the cases.
192 divided by 263.
Multiply by 100 and round.
questions.onCorrect: A's rate on large stones is 73 percent, lower than its 93 percent on small stones, because large stones are harder.

misconceptions.feedback: That is A's pooled rate over all stones.
That is A's rate on small stones.

questions.prompt: Which variable is a likely confounder for the effect of coffee on heart disease?
hints: A confounder influences both coffee drinking and heart disease.
Which of these is linked to both?

acceptedIdeas: Smoking
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Smoking

questions.onCorrect: Smoking is associated with coffee drinking and with heart disease, so it can create or hide an apparent link between them.

misconceptions.feedback: Mug colour has no known link with heart disease.
The day of data entry affects neither coffee drinking nor the heart.
The number of rows is a property of the dataset, not of the people in it.

choices.label: The day of the week the data were entered
The number of rows in the table
The colour of the mug
Smoking

questions.prompt: What name is given to a reversal where the pooled comparison disagrees with every subgroup?
hints: It is named after a statistician who described it in 1951.
Its name is a surname plus the word paradox.

acceptedIdeas: Simpson's paradox
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Simpson's paradox

questions.onCorrect: Simpson's paradox arises when the mix of subgroups differs between the arms, so the pooled and subgroup comparisons can point opposite ways.

misconceptions.feedback: A confounder is the cause of the reversal here. The reversal itself has a name of its own.

questions.prompt: What is the shape X ← Z → Y called, in which one variable causes two others?
hints: The arrows leave Z in two directions.
Its name suggests a utensil with prongs.

acceptedIdeas: fork
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fork

questions.onCorrect: In a fork, X and Y are associated through Z even if neither affects the other, and comparing units with equal Z blocks the association.

misconceptions.feedback: A chain runs in one direction, X to M to Y. This shape has one variable at the root of two arrows.

questions.prompt: What is the middle variable M called in the chain X → M → Y?
hints: It carries the effect from X to Y.
Its name comes from the word for something in the middle.

acceptedIdeas: mediator
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: mediator

questions.onCorrect: A mediator carries part or all of the effect of X on Y, so adjusting for it removes what you want to measure.

misconceptions.feedback: A confounder causes both X and Y. The variable asked about lies between them.

questions.prompt: Talent and looks both raise the chance of becoming famous, and in the whole population they are unrelated. What happens to the relationship between talent and looks if you look only at famous people?
hints: Fame is an effect of both talent and looks.
Think about how someone with little talent became famous.

acceptedIdeas: They become negatively related, because a person with little of one needs a lot of the other
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They become negatively related, because a person with little of one needs a lot of the other

questions.onCorrect: Two causes that are unrelated become related once you select on their shared effect, which is why a collider must not be conditioned on.

misconceptions.feedback: Selecting on a variable that both traits cause does change it. Among the famous, a person with little talent must have had looks to get there, and the reverse.
Fame can come from either trait, so a person with little of one needs a lot of the other. That produces a negative link, not a positive one.

choices.label: They become negatively related, because a person with little of one needs a lot of the other
They stay unrelated, because selecting people cannot change how two traits go together
They become positively related, because famous people are high in both

questions.prompt: You want the total effect of X on Y. Why should M be left alone?
hints: Where is M in the graph relative to X and Y?
What does adjusting for a variable do to a path through it?

acceptedIdeas: M lies on the causal path from X to Y, and adjusting for it would block part of the effect.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: M lies on the causal path from X to Y, and adjusting for it would block part of the effect.

questions.onCorrect: M carries part of the effect of X on Y, so holding it fixed would remove that part from the estimate.

misconceptions.feedback: M has one arrow in and one out. A collider has two arrows pointing into it.
Adjusting for a mediator removes the effect we are trying to measure, and a collider adds bias.

choices.label: Adjusting for M is always harmless.
M lies on the causal path from X to Y, and adjusting for it would block part of the effect.
M is a collider.

questions.prompt: In the graph X ← Z → Y, X ← W → Y, X ← V → Y and X → M → Y, how many backdoor paths from X to Y need blocking?
hints: A backdoor path starts with an arrow pointing into X.
Count the common causes of X and Y.
The path through M leaves X, so it is not a backdoor path.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of Z, W and V gives a backdoor path that starts with an arrow into X, and X → M → Y is the causal path, so there are 3.

questions.onCorrect: The three common causes each give a backdoor path, so Z, W and V all belong in the adjustment set, and M does not.

misconceptions.feedback: The path through M leaves X rather than entering it, so it is the causal path.
Each of Z, W and V gives its own backdoor path.

questions.prompt: In the graph Z → X, Z → Y, X → Y, X → C and Y → C, with C a collider, which variables should be adjusted for to estimate the effect of X on Y?
hints: List the paths from X to Y that start with an arrow into X.
A collider blocks the path through it unless you adjust for it.

acceptedIdeas: Z alone, because it is the only common cause of X and Y
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Z alone, because it is the only common cause of X and Y

questions.onCorrect: Adjusting for the collider C would have opened a false path from X to Y, so only Z is adjusted for.

misconceptions.feedback: Adjusting for the collider C would open the path X → C ← Y, which is blocked while C is left alone, and so it would introduce bias.
The path X ← Z → Y is a backdoor path. It carries an association that is not the effect of X, and it stays open unless Z is adjusted for.
C is a collider. Adjusting for it opens a false path between X and Y, and the backdoor path through Z would still be open.

choices.label: C alone, because it is affected by both X and Y
Z alone, because it is the only common cause of X and Y
No variable, because X → Y is already a causal path
Z and C

questions.prompt: In X ← Z → Y, X ← W → Y and X → M → Y, how many backdoor paths from X to Y need blocking?
hints: A backdoor path starts with an arrow pointing into X.
Count the common causes of X and Y.
The path through M leaves X.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The backdoor paths are X ← Z → Y and X ← W → Y, which start with an arrow into X, and X → M → Y is the causal path. There are 2.

questions.onCorrect: The adjustment set is Z and W, and M is left alone so that the causal path stays open.

misconceptions.feedback: The path through M is the causal path, not a backdoor path.
There are two common causes, Z and W, so two backdoor paths.

questions.prompt: What is a variable called when two arrows point into it?
hints: The two arrows meet at the variable.
Talent and looks both point into fame.

acceptedIdeas: collider
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: collider

questions.onCorrect: Conditioning on a collider opens a path that was blocked, and can create an association between its causes.

misconceptions.feedback: A mediator has one arrow in and one out. This variable has two arrows in.

questions.prompt: You want the total effect of X on Y, and M lies on the path X → M → Y. Should you adjust for M?
hints: M lies between X and Y.
What does adjusting do to a path?

acceptedIdeas: No, it carries part of the effect
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, it carries part of the effect

questions.onCorrect: Adjusting for M blocks the causal path through it, so the estimate would leave out the effect that travels via M.

misconceptions.feedback: Adjusting for every available variable is not safe. A mediator carries part of the effect.
Whether M is binary does not change that it lies on the path from X to Y.
A large sample does not change what a variable does to a path.

choices.label: No, it carries part of the effect
Only if M is binary
Only if the sample is large
Yes, always

questions.prompt: What is the name for a situation in which a rule or an accident assigns exposure as if at random, without anyone running a trial?
hints: The assignment is done by nature or circumstance, not by the researcher.
Think of nature or circumstance running the experiment.

acceptedIdeas: natural experiment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: natural experiment

questions.onCorrect: A natural experiment is only as good as its as-if randomness, which cannot be tested directly.

misconceptions.feedback: In a randomised trial the researcher flips the coin. Here nobody does.

questions.prompt: A scheme is offered to one group, whose scores rise from 50 to 56. A similar group that is left alone sees its scores rise from 48 to 50. How much of the treated group's rise of 6 would you credit to the scheme?
hints: The group that was left alone shows what happens with no scheme.
Take the change that would have happened anyway away from the treated change.

acceptedIdeas: About 4, which is the rise of 6 less the 2 that happened without the scheme
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 4, which is the rise of 6 less the 2 that happened without the scheme

questions.onCorrect: The treated group rose by 6 and the group left alone by 2, so only 6 − 2 = 4 of the rise can be credited to the scheme.

misconceptions.feedback: The group that was left alone rose by 2 without the scheme, so some of the treated group's rise would probably have happened anyway.
A rise of 2 is what happened without the scheme. It is the part to take away from the treated rise, not the effect itself.
Both groups rose, but the treated group rose by 6 and the other by only 2. The extra 4 is what the scheme can be credited with.

choices.label: None, because both groups rose
About 4, which is the rise of 6 less the 2 that happened without the scheme
About 2, which is the rise in the group that was left alone
All 6, because the scheme is the only difference between the groups

questions.prompt: Treated: 40 to 46. Control: 38 to 41. What is the difference in differences, treated change minus control change?
hints: Find each group's change first.
Each change is the after value minus the before value.
Subtract the control change from the treated change.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The treated change is 6 and the control change is 3, so 6 − 3 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: The treatment is credited with 3 of the 6, since the control group rose by 3 anyway.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treated change alone. Subtract the control change.
That adds the changes. Subtract the control change instead.

questions.prompt: In the treated group scores fell by 3, yet the estimate is positive. Why?
hints: Compare the treated change with the control change.
What would have happened to the treated group without treatment?

acceptedIdeas: The control group fell by 8, so without treatment the treated group would probably have fallen by more.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The control group fell by 8, so without treatment the treated group would probably have fallen by more.

questions.onCorrect: The control fell by 8, so the treated fall of 3 is 5 better than the trend, and the difference in differences is +5.

misconceptions.feedback: The fall is real. What it means depends on the trend the control group shows.
Nothing cancels. The estimate is the treated change minus the control change.

choices.label: The control group fell by 8, so without treatment the treated group would probably have fallen by more.
The treated group did not really fall.
Negative changes cancel out.

questions.prompt: Treated: 80 to 83. Control: 70 to 78. What is the difference in differences?
hints: Find each group's change.
Treated +3, control +8.
Subtract the control change from the treated change.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The treated change is +3 and the control change is +8, so 3 − 8 = −5.

questions.onCorrect: The treated group rose less than the control group did, so the treatment is credited with a fall of 5.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign matters. The treated group rose by less than the control, so the estimate is negative.
That adds the changes. Subtract instead.

questions.prompt: After a policy change, the treated region's index went from 120 to 110 and the control region's from 100 to 96. What is the difference in differences?
hints: Find each change, with its sign.
Treated −10, control −4.
Subtract the control change from the treated change.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The treated change is −10 and the control change is −4, so −10 − (−4) = −6.

questions.onCorrect: The index fell 6 more in the treated region than the trend in the control region would explain.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treated change alone. Subtract the control change, −4.
That adds the changes. Subtract the control change instead.

questions.prompt: Treated: 45 to 41. Control: 50 to 42. What is the difference in differences (treated change minus control change)?
hints: Find each change with its sign.
Treated −4, control −8.
Subtract the control change from the treated change.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The treated change is −4 and the control change is −8, so −4 − (−8) = +4.

questions.onCorrect: The treated group fell by 4 less than the trend in the control group suggests.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treated change alone. Subtract the control change.
That adds the changes. Subtract the control change instead.

questions.prompt: What does a difference-in-differences estimate rely on?
hints: The control group stands in for what would have happened to the treated group.
Its change is subtracted as the trend.

acceptedIdeas: The groups would have changed equally without treatment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The groups would have changed equally without treatment

questions.onCorrect: The estimate treats the control change as what the treated group would have done without treatment, the parallel-trends assumption.

misconceptions.feedback: The levels may differ. Only the changes are compared.
A large sample does not make the trends parallel.
Random assignment is not required, which is why the method is used where it is not possible.

choices.label: The groups would have changed equally without treatment
The sample is large
The treated group was chosen at random
The groups started at equal levels

questions.prompt: What is the name of the design that compares people just above and just below an eligibility cut-off?
hints: It looks at a jump in the outcome at the cut-off.
The name has two words, the first one a kind of line fitting.

acceptedIdeas: regression discontinuity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: regression discontinuity

questions.onCorrect: People just either side of the cut-off are nearly alike, so a jump in the outcome there can be read as the effect.

misconceptions.feedback: That design compares changes over time in two groups. This one compares people either side of a cut-off.

questions.prompt: How many of the nine samples have a mean of exactly 4?
hints: Write the nine ordered pairs out and average each.
A mean of 4 needs the two values to add to 8.
Which pairs from 2, 4 and 6 add to 8? Order matters here.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The samples (2, 6), (4, 4) and (6, 2) all average 4, so 3 of the 9.

questions.onCorrect: A mean of 4 is the most common outcome, which is why the nine means pile up around the population mean.

misconceptions.feedback: Only (4, 4) was counted. The pairs (2, 6) and (6, 2) also add to 8.
Check the order: (2, 6) and (6, 2) are different samples, and (4, 4) is a third.

questions.prompt: The population variance is 8/3, about 2.67. What do you expect the variance of the nine sample means to be, to two decimal places?
hints: Compare how far apart the means are with how far apart the data are.
The means are bunched more tightly than the data, so the answer is below 2.67.
Try dividing the population variance by the sample size.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Averaging two values halves the variance: (8/3) / 2 = 4/3, about 1.33.

questions.onCorrect: The variance of the means is exactly the population variance divided by n, here 8/3 divided by 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the population variance. The means vary less than single draws do.
The variance of the means is smaller, not larger, than the variance of the data.

questions.prompt: What is the probability that all 20 independent 95 percent intervals cover the true mean? Give a decimal to two places.
hints: Independent events multiply.
Multiply 0.95 by itself 20 times.
Use 0.95^20 on a calculator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each covers with probability 0.95, so all 20 cover with 0.95^20, which is 0.358, about 0.36.

questions.onCorrect: A run of 20 successes is a bit less likely than not to avoid a miss, so one miss in a set of twenty is entirely ordinary.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for a single interval. All twenty must cover, so multiply 20 times.
That is the chance a single interval misses.

questions.prompt: A study with a power of 0.3 fails to reject the null. If a real effect of the size it was planned for does exist, what is the chance the study misses it?
hints: The study either catches a real effect or misses it.
The two chances add to 1.
Subtract the power from 1.
questions.onCorrect: A study this weak misses a real effect 70 percent of the time, so its failure to reject says little.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of catching it. The question asks about missing it.
The threshold, alpha, is about false alarms. A miss is a different error.

questions.prompt: A researcher slices the data 30 ways, and nothing is going on. What is the probability that at least one slice gives p below 0.05, to two decimals?
hints: Each slice is a test at alpha 0.05.
The chance that none of the 30 rejects is 0.95^30.
Subtract it from 1.
questions.onCorrect: More than three times in four, a slice with p below 0.05 will turn up by chance, so finding one proves little.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for a single slice. There are 30 chances.
That is the chance that no slice rejects. Subtract it from 1.

questions.prompt: The line height = 79.7 + 6 × age was fitted to children aged 4 to 10. What height, in cm, does it give at age 40?
hints: Put 40 in place of age.
Add the intercept 79.7.
questions.onCorrect: 319.7 cm is not a possible height. The line only describes the ages it was fitted on.

misconceptions.feedback: That omits the intercept of 79.7.
That is the height at age 10. The question asks for age 40.

questions.prompt: What do we call the arm of a study that does not receive the treatment and serves as the comparison?
hints: It is the group the treated arm is compared with.
Its name begins with the word for keeping something in check.

acceptedIdeas: control group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: control group

questions.onCorrect: Without a control group there is nothing to compare the treated group against.

misconceptions.feedback: A placebo is a dummy treatment given to some people. The arm that is compared against has a different name.

questions.prompt: What is a variable called when two arrows point into it?
hints: The two arrows meet at the variable.
Its name suggests particles meeting head on.

acceptedIdeas: collider
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: collider

questions.onCorrect: Two causes that are unrelated become related once you select on their shared effect, which is why a collider must not be conditioned on.

misconceptions.feedback: A confounder has arrows leaving it. This variable receives two arrows.

questions.prompt: The control group went from 48 to 50 with no treatment. By how much did scores rise because of time and other outside causes alone?
hints: The control group did not get the treatment.
Its change is the change from outside causes.
Subtract before from after.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The control group changed by 50 − 48 = 2, and with no treatment that is the change due to everything else.

questions.onCorrect: The treated group rose by 6, so only 6 − 2 = 4 of its rise can be credited to the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treated group's change, which includes the treatment.
That is the control group's level after, not its change.

flashcards.front: What do we call the standard deviation of a sample mean?
flashcards.back: It is the standard error, equal to the population sd divided by the square root of n.

acceptedIdeas: standard error
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: standard error

flashcards.front: The sd is 10 and n = 25. What is the standard error?
Why does doubling the sample size not halve the standard error?
flashcards.back: The error falls with the square root of n, so doubling n divides it by only about 1.41.

flashcards.front: What is the z-score of a value x, given a mean and sd?
flashcards.back: z = (x − mean) / sd, the distance from the mean counted in standard deviations.

acceptedIdeas: (x − mean) / sd
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (x − mean) / sd

flashcards.front: The mean is 100 and the sd is 20. What is the z-score of 140?
Why is the height of a normal curve not a probability?
flashcards.back: Only area under the curve is a probability, and a single value has area zero.

flashcards.front: What is the margin of error for a mean?
flashcards.back: It is the critical value times the standard error, and it is the half-width of the interval.

acceptedIdeas: critical value times standard error
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: critical value times standard error

flashcards.front: n = 49, sigma = 14 known. What is the standard error?
Why does a 99 percent interval come out wider than a 95 percent interval from the same data?
flashcards.back: A larger multiplier is needed to be more confident of covering the mean, so the margin grows.

flashcards.front: A method is 95 percent confident. What does the 95 percent describe?
flashcards.back: It describes the method: in repeated samples, about 95 percent of the intervals it produces cover the true value.

flashcards.front: 42 of 120 support a plan. What is the sample proportion, as a decimal?
What is the standard error of a proportion?
flashcards.back: It is sqrt(p̂ (1 − p̂) / n), which depends on how mixed the answers are and on n.

acceptedIdeas: sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: sqrt(p(1-p)/n)

flashcards.front: What does a p-value measure?
flashcards.back: It is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true.

flashcards.front: The claimed mean is 100, sigma is 15, n = 36 and the sample mean is 104. What is z?
A test gives p = 0.2. Does that prove there is no effect?
flashcards.back: No, the data were simply not surprising enough, which can also happen when the sample is small.

flashcards.front: What is a Type I error?
flashcards.back: It is rejecting a null hypothesis that is true, a false alarm, which happens at rate alpha.

acceptedIdeas: rejecting a true null
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: rejecting a true null

flashcards.front: In 100 runs with a real effect, a test catches it 80 times. What is the power?
flashcards.back: The power is the share of real effects caught, 80 / 100 = 0.8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The power is the share of real effects caught, 80 / 100 = 0.8.

flashcards.front: Why is lowering alpha not free?
flashcards.back: With the sample size fixed, a stricter cut-off misses more real effects, so beta rises.

flashcards.front: How is the distance of a real effect from zero measured in a power calculation?
flashcards.back: In standard errors, as effect / (sd / sqrt(n)).

flashcards.front: The calculation gives n = 41.2. What sample size do you plan?
flashcards.back: Round up to 42, since 41 would leave the power slightly below the target.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Round up to 42, since 41 would leave the power slightly below the target.

flashcards.front: What are the four things power depends on?
flashcards.back: It depends on the size of the effect, the spread, the sample size and alpha.

flashcards.front: How do you find the standard error of a difference between two independent means?
flashcards.back: Add the squared standard errors and take the square root, because variances add.

flashcards.front: Two means have standard errors 3 and 4. What is the standard error of their difference?
flashcards.back: sqrt(3² + 4²) = sqrt(25) = 5.

flashcards.front: When is a paired analysis appropriate?
flashcards.back: When each observation in one group is matched to one in the other, as with the same people measured twice.

flashcards.front: What is the chance of at least one false rejection in m independent tests of true nulls at alpha?
flashcards.back: It is 1 − (1 − alpha)^m, which rises quickly with m.

flashcards.front: Bonferroni: 20 tests with an overall alpha of 0.05. What is the per-test threshold?
What counts as the number of tests when a result is picked after looking at the data?
flashcards.back: Every comparison that could have been reported, including the ones that were looked at and dropped.

flashcards.front: What does a least-squares line minimise?
flashcards.back: It minimises the sum of the squared vertical gaps between the points and the line.

flashcards.front: The slope is 2 and the mean of x and y are 3 and 10. What is the intercept?
flashcards.back: intercept = ȳ − slope × x̄ = 10 − 2 × 3 = 4.

flashcards.front: What is a residual?
flashcards.back: It is the observed value minus the value the line predicts at that x.

flashcards.front: What does random assignment make possible that random sampling does not?
flashcards.back: It supports a causal claim about the treatment, whereas random sampling supports generalising to a population.

flashcards.front: How many ways can 4 of 6 people be chosen for the treated group? (6 × 5 × 4 × 3 / 4!)
flashcards.back: The count is 360 / 24 = 15.

flashcards.front: What is the name for hiding the arm from participants?
flashcards.back: It is called blinding, and it stops expectation from shaping the outcome.

acceptedIdeas: blinding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: blinding

flashcards.front: What is a confounder?
flashcards.back: It is a variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome, which can create or hide an apparent effect.

acceptedIdeas: confounder
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: confounder

flashcards.front: Does collecting more data remove confounding?
flashcards.back: No, because the confounder still drives both the treatment and the outcome in every extra observation.

flashcards.front: A succeeded in 90 of 100 cases. What is the rate as a percentage?
flashcards.back: 90 / 100 = 0.90, which is 90 percent.

flashcards.front: What is a collider?
flashcards.back: It is a variable with two arrows pointing into it, and conditioning on it can create a false association.

acceptedIdeas: collider
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: collider

flashcards.front: What is a backdoor path from X to Y?
flashcards.back: It is a path that starts with an arrow into X, such as X ← Z → Y, and it has to be blocked to read an effect.

flashcards.front: Should you adjust for a mediator when you want the total effect?
flashcards.back: No, because the mediator carries part of the effect and adjusting blocks it.

flashcards.front: What is a difference in differences?
flashcards.back: It is the treated group's change minus the control group's change, which removes the trend they share.

flashcards.front: Treated 10 to 15, control 10 to 12. What is the difference in differences?
flashcards.back: The treated change is 5 and the control change is 2, so 5 − 2 = 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The treated change is 5 and the control change is 2, so 5 − 2 = 3.

flashcards.front: What must a control group have done for difference in differences to work?
flashcards.back: It must have followed the same trend the treated group would have followed without treatment.
